digests.author: Howard Marks
digests.title: A Layman Thinks About AI
digests.summary: Howard Marks examines whether investors should invest in AI and whether they can do so intelligently. He disclaims tech expertise but argues investors cannot abstain from thinking about AI because it may be the most impactful development ever. Marks stresses that investing requires positioning for the future, but AI involves unusually many critical variables—technology evolution, compute demand, competitive structure, beneficiaries, financing, timing—making accurate forecasting exceptionally difficult. He poses questions about how AI works, its capabilities, profitability, competitive landscape, and data-center economics. He notes AI is a small part of the U.S. economy yet drives an outsized share of growth and market gains, creating concentration risk. Credit markets have seen nearly $600 billion in AI-related debt issuance this year, with potential crowding-out effects. Marks defines a bubble as irrational exuberance leading to imprudent behavior and excessive prices, concluding that judging whether AI is a bubble depends on unknowable factors. He recommends calibrated humility, careful position sizing, and acting despite uncertainty rather than paralysis.
key_points: AI is potentially the most consequential and least predictable development for investors in at least a generation.
Investing in AI requires correctly assessing many variables simultaneously, making the combined probability of success unusually low.
AI is a small part of the U.S. economy but contributes disproportionately to growth, earnings, and stock market gains, creating concentration risk.
AI-related debt issuance has totaled nearly $600 billion globally this year, representing over one-fifth of U.S. IG supply.
Data centers are not a "layup"; they face constraints like power, cooling, financing, and overbuilding risk.
Frontier labs are rated as highly unpredictable, near "binary," yet are priced at a premium.
Marks concludes that whether AI is a bubble is currently a matter of faith, and intelligent investing requires calibrated humility and price discipline.

quotes.point: Underscores why investors cannot abstain despite uncertainty.
quotes.text: AI is the biggest development of our time and could be one of the most impactful things the world has ever seen

quotes.point: Highlights systemic concentration risk across portfolios.
quotes.text: The sum of these trends has left the S&P 500 highly concentrated in a few AI and tech companies.

quotes.point: Warns against both ignorance and overconfidence in AI.
quotes.text: Two kinds of investors lose a lot of money: those who know nothing and those who know everything.

implications.text: Scrutinize AI-linked IG and HY exposure; recognize that AI debt now constitutes roughly 12% of the Bloomberg USD IG Corporate index.
Stress-test portfolios for AI concentration, given that 42 AI-related companies generated around two-thirds of S&P 500 gains since January 2024.
Assess data-center credits for lease "out clauses," chip collateral durability, and circular transaction linkages before extending exposure.
Watch whether rate-insensitive AI borrowers elevate government borrowing costs, altering the macro rate backdrop.
Adopt calibrated humility in AI allocations: size positions small, diversify across predictability tiers, and demand price discipline rather than betting on binary outcomes.

digests.author: Ben Inker and John Pease
digests.title: A Catalyst for the AI Bubble Break
digests.summary: GMO's Ben Inker and John Pease argue that the catalyst for a potential AI bubble break may come from equity supply rather than disappointing AI demand. Bubbles need fresh capital, and rising supply often breaks them. They point to the June 12, 2027 release of roughly $2 trillion of SpaceX shares from lockup, likely IPOs from Anthropic and OpenAI together valued at about 5% of the U.S. stock market, and hyperscaler-driven secondary issuance. They argue passive, benchmark-aware and constrained markets leave fewer buyers willing to absorb new equity supply. GMO estimates that each 1% increase in equity supply has historically cut market value by roughly 4% over the next year. With equity supply moving from shrinking about 1% per annum to increasing close to 5%, they say returns could be some 20% below average over the next 12-18 months from supply alone, before considering expensive valuations and other risks. They caution this is not guaranteed, but say prices are likely to turn before weak AI economics become obvious.
key_points: GMO argues the AI bubble's catalyst may be equity supply rather than disappointing AI demand.
SpaceX lockup release of roughly $2 trillion is expected on June 12, 2027.
Likely IPOs from Anthropic and OpenAI are together valued at about 5% of the U.S. stock market over the next 12 months.
Hyperscaler capex is producing net dilution; GMO says equity supply may move from shrinking about 1% per annum to increasing close to 5%.
GMO estimates each 1% increase in equity supply has historically cut market value by roughly 4% over the next year.
Passive, benchmark-aware and constrained markets leave fewer opportunistic buyers; GMO says only 30 cents of every equity dollar is used opportunistically.
GMO says supply alone could imply returns some 20% below average over 12-18 months, before valuations and other risks.

quotes.point: Frames equity supply as the potential trigger for the AI bubble break.
quotes.text: Bubbles need fresh capital, and rising supply often breaks them.

quotes.point: GMO's central quantitative estimate for the supply headwind.
quotes.text: each 1% increase in equity supply has historically cut market value by roughly 4% over the next year.

quotes.point: Suggests market prices may fall before weak AI economics become obvious.
quotes.text: prices are likely to turn before the market truly knows that has happened.

implications.text: Add the U.S. equity-supply calendar to the macro watchlist: SpaceX lockup release on June 12, 2027, Anthropic/OpenAI IPOs, and hyperscaler issuance.
Stress-test North's U.S. equity exposure against GMO's scenario of returns roughly 20% below average over 12-18 months from supply alone, treating the 4x multiplier as an estimate.
Monitor flow sensitivity and liquidity: GMO argues constrained, benchmark-aware and passive markets have fewer opportunistic buyers to absorb new supply.
Remember GMO's catalyst is a hypothesis; verify issuance data and do not present the 20% estimate as guaranteed.
Treat this as a risk/reward shift, not an arbitrage signal; avoid assuming the market can absorb each supply round without a hiccup.

digests.author: Howard Marks (Oaktree Capital Management)
digests.title: Shall We Repeal the Laws of Economics – Part III
digests.summary: Marks returns to his 2024 and 2025 critique of governments trying to override the laws of economics, arguing that economies are natural organisms whose steering produces distortions and unintended second-order effects. The trigger is the U.S. Treasury's August 2026 decision to at least double the maximum size of long-dated buybacks (from $2 billion to $4 billion per operation), later tripled to $6 billion, with Secretary Bessent hinting at a 'whatever-it-takes' approach after the 30-year yield closed above 5.3%, a 19-year high. Marks calls this cosmetic: the effect may be fleeting, it does not address the root causes (stubborn 3.7% PCE inflation, elevated oil prices tied to the Iran war, a deficit near 6% of GDP with 4% unemployment, over $1 trillion of net interest, roughly $2 trillion of net issuance, and multi-trillion AI-driven capital demand), and market reaction has been muted. He quotes Druckenmiller and Buffett on the unsustainability, doubts a dollar debt default, discusses 'the debasement trade', and prescribes fiscal discipline, revenue increases and faster GDP growth rather than selling U.S. stocks.
key_points: Treasury's August 2026 expansion of long-dated buybacks (to $4bn, then $6bn per operation) is framed by Marks as an attempt to improve the interest-rate picture cosmetically, not to solve the underlying problem.
The 30-year Treasury closed above 5.3% on August 17, a 19-year high; long rates fell immediately after the announcement but bounced back the next day.

Root causes cited: PCE inflation of 3.7% in July versus a 2% target, oil prices tied to the Iran war, a deficit near 6% of GDP with 4% unemployment, net interest outlays above $1 trillion, roughly $2 trillion of net issuance, and heavy AI-related capital demand (McKinsey: over $5 trillion worldwide through 2030).
Marks sides with Druckenmiller and against Bessent's claim that yields don't reflect fundamentals, and cites Evercore ISI's September 9 note that markets were 'underwhelmed' by the buyback reveal.

He sees no serious probability of a U.S. default because debt is denominated in dollars, and doubts the dollar loses reserve status soon (89% of FX transactions, 57% of allocated reserves), while noting gold recently surpassed the dollar as the leading central bank reserve asset.
The only genuine solution is behavioural: fiscal responsibility, higher revenues as a share of GDP, spending growth below GDP growth, and productivity gains from AI and pro-business policy.
He does not recommend selling U.S. stocks, since the problem is fiscal and dollar-related; diversification into non-dollar or non-financial assets carries its own risks and may be premature.

quotes.point: Druckenmiller's line, endorsed by Marks, frames yield suppression as deferring adjustment rather than solving it — a warning against reading policy support as all-clear.
quotes.text: Every basis point of artificial yield suppression is a subsidy to procrastination.

quotes.point: Caps the memo's core framing: higher long yields are a chronic cost to be paid, not a dislocation to be traded as an anomaly.
quotes.text: If the 30-year must trade at 5.5% to clear, that isn't a crisis. It is an invoice.

quotes.point: Marks' analogy for why intervention addresses symptoms; it argues against positioning for a durable policy-driven decline in long rates.
quotes.text: Forcing rates down by buying bonds is like a doctor applying an ice pack to a patient with a fever.

implications.text: Treat the August–September 2026 Treasury buyback expansion as cosmetic, not a regime change: the memo's list of rate drivers (3.7% PCE, oil/Iran, ~6% deficit, ~$2tn net issuance, AI capex) argues against forecasting a durable decline in long-end yields.

Do not sell U.S. equities on this memo alone — Marks explicitly says the problem is fiscal and dollar-related, not a problem with U.S. companies, and that non-U.S. alternatives carry their own growth, scale and regulation risks.

Flag the 'debasement trade' and the FT's point that Treasury yield suppression may weaken the dollar: review IDR/USD exposure and whether dollar-denominated assets in the South book are truly a hedge or the same risk in another form.

Remember that diversification away from the dollar is not costless and may look wrong for a long time, since no one knows whether or when the fiscal issue comes to a head; size any non-dollar or gold allocation accordingly and note the memo's caveat that no other currency is clearly a substitute.

Keep the memo's asymmetry in mind: an acute event (failed auction, buyers' strike) is judged improbable, while the cost is chronic and already being imposed — so monitor 30-year yields as an ongoing drag on valuation rather than a single tail event.

digests.author: Lucas White
digests.title: The Electricity Tipping Point & the Next Energy Boom
digests.summary: Lucas White argues that global electricity demand is surging, ending the era of relatively flat U.S. demand. AI and non-AI data centers, electrification, and industrial and commercial usage are driving growth, though data centers are expected to drive less than 10% of global electricity demand growth over the next few years. U.S. electricity prices have shot up almost 50% since 2020, with UK and European prices rising even more, after decades of minimal investment left grids strained. White says massive investment in generation and grid expansion is required. Natural gas benefits from a U.S. shale glut and limited export capacity, with LNG projects under construction set to double export capacity. Nuclear has staged a remarkable turnaround, and uranium deficits are expected in the 2030s. Renewables accounted for over 90% of U.S. power capacity additions last year, with storage addressing intermittency. Grid modernization, batteries and storage, and commodities such as lithium, nickel, cobalt and copper are key. Energy efficiency becomes financially attractive at high prices. White concludes that energy is the foundation of the economy and that countries leading the electricity race will have a massive edge in AI.
key_points: U.S. electricity demand, flat for decades, is now growing as AI and non-AI data centers, electrification, and industrial/commercial usage overwhelm efficiency gains; data centers are expected to drive less than 10% of global demand growth.
U.S. electricity prices have risen almost 50% since 2020, and UK/European prices more, after decades of minimal investment left grids strained on both generation and T&D.
Natural gas: a U.S. shale glut and limited export capacity create a global price disconnect; LNG projects under construction will double U.S. export capacity and approved projects could triple it.

Nuclear has turned around on clean baseload demand; uranium demand is projected to double by 2040 while existing mine output is expected to halve between 2030 and 2040, implying deficits in the 2030s.

Renewables supplied over 90% of U.S. power capacity additions last year; battery attachment rates for solar have risen from zero to 70–80%, and storage demand is broadening beyond EVs to grid and data centers.

Commodities remain central: lithium deficits are expected in the next couple of years, and copper deficits later this decade and in the 2030s; energy efficiency also becomes financially attractive with high power prices.

quotes.point: Flags the scale of electricity price pressure since 2020.
quotes.text: prices have shot up almost 50% since 2020

quotes.point: States the letter's uranium supply-deficit thesis.
quotes.text: deficits are expected to be the norm in the uranium market as we move into the 2030s

quotes.point: Frames electricity as a strategic macro and AI competitiveness issue.
quotes.text: countries that lead the electricity race will have a massive edge in AI

implications.text: Remember the letter's claim that energy is the foundation of the economy and that countries leading the electricity race gain a massive edge in AI; track electricity demand, price and grid-investment data as macro inputs.

Review the USD book for indirect exposure to the letter's themes—U.S. natural gas/LNG, uranium, grid equipment, storage and copper—while noting the letter is thematic research, not a security recommendation.

Check the Indonesia book against the letter's point that emerging-market demand revolves more around economic development and infrastructure expansion; assess relevance of grid buildout and commodity demand.

Note the letter's grid-reliability example—the Spain/Portugal outage that left over 50 million people without electricity for almost 20 hours—and consider reliability and concentration risks in energy-transition exposure.
Treat the thesis as secular and long-dated: the letter says natural gas turbines are sold out for years and a nuclear project may take a decade, and it asks investors to sift through neglected areas.

digests.author: Tina Vandersteel (GMO, Head of Emerging Country Debt)
digests.title: Targeting Outcomes: Taking a Total Return Approach to Emerging Market Debt
digests.summary: A GMO Q&A with Tina Vandersteel, Head of Emerging Country Debt, on launching a Total Return EMD strategy in a mutual fund format, targeting SOFR + 3% rather than a benchmark-relative objective. She argues benchmark-relative fixed income forces investors to inherit benchmark duration, yield, credit quality and currency exposure, and that EMD benchmarks can drift in duration, offer limited credit-quality control and cover only part of the investable universe. The total return approach instead starts from the return hurdle and builds the portfolio from the bottom up across a funded bond/loan portion plus FX and rates overlay programmes. On valuation, she says the dollar is 'quite rich' versus EM currencies and local currency rates offer high total return potential even without currency appreciation, with more local markets priced to deliver SOFR + 3% than in decades; by contrast, sovereign, quasi-sovereign and corporate credit spreads look narrow. Expected duration is 3-4 years, credit skewed to BB and below, with shorting and credit protection for downside. She frames the strategy as complementary, not a replacement, and notes greater tracking error and governance demands.
key_points: GMO is extending its Emerging Country Debt offerings with a Total Return strategy in a mutual fund format, targeting cash-relative SOFR + 3%.

Vandersteel says benchmark-relative investors inherit benchmark duration, yield, credit quality and currency exposure, and EMD benchmarks can drift in duration, limit credit-quality control and represent only part of the universe.
The strategy has two building blocks: a funded asset portion of bonds and loans/private instruments, plus derivatives-based FX and rates overlays run as portable alpha.
The dollar is described as 'quite rich' relative to EM currencies, and local currency rates are said to offer high total return potential before any currency appreciation.
The combination of cheap currencies and high rates has, in GMO's view, priced more local currency markets to deliver SOFR + 3% than has been true in decades.
Aggregate sovereign, quasi-sovereign and corporate credit spreads appear narrow relative to the broader opportunity set, though GMO still finds attractive individual issues.
Expected duration is a mix of hard and local currency in the 3-4 year range; the hurdle could tilt credit quality to BB and below, with shorting and credit protection used for downside.
A benchmark-agnostic approach requires tolerance for tracking error, peer dispersion and unconventional reporting, and depends on the investor's governance framework.

quotes.point: GMO's stated FX valuation view underpinning the local currency opportunity set.
quotes.text: The dollar is currently quite rich relative to EM currencies

quotes.point: The core bullish claim for local currency EMD as a total return source.
quotes.text: the combination of cheap currencies and high rates has priced more local currency markets to deliver SOFR + 3% than has been true in decades

quotes.point: Contrasts with the local currency view; flags limited compensation in hard currency credit broadly.
quotes.text: aggregate sovereign, quasi-sovereign, and corporate credit spreads appear narrow relative to the broader opportunity set

implications.text: Log GMO's view that the dollar is rich versus EM currencies and that local rates plus cheap FX price many markets to SOFR + 3% — a stance to track, not to adopt without the desk's own valuation work.

The IDR book sits in the local currency EMD universe GMO describes as unusually well valued on rates and FX; check whether current South positioning is consistent with that claim or deliberately differs, and note the document names no country or issuer specifics.

Note the contrast between local currency (cheap currencies, high rates) and hard currency credit (narrow aggregate spreads); any USD EM credit exposure should be judged issue by issue rather than on index-level spread.

Record the implementation risks the letter itself flags: a SOFR + 3% hurdle points to BB and below credit, 3-4 year duration, and possible shorting or credit protection — plus tracking error and peer dispersion for benchmark-agnostic mandates.

Treat this as a framework memo, not a trade idea: it argues total return versus benchmark-relative mandates, so it is relevant to how Six South sets objectives and benchmarks rather than to any single position.

digests.author: Howard Marks
digests.title: What’s Going on in Private Credit?
digests.summary: Howard Marks traces the evolution of credit markets from non-investment-grade debt and LBOs through broadly syndicated loans, securitization, alternative investments, direct lending, and the recent marketing of direct lending vehicles to individual and retirement investors. He argues that novel investment forms often follow a pattern: early rewards, growing envy and capital, lower standards, and eventual disillusionment. Marks applies this to direct lending, where roughly $2 trillion of loans have been made in 15 years, much by managers untested in rough times. He highlights software debt, including ARR loans and high leverage, as a growing concern after AI-related disruption affected sentiment. He also discusses redemption limits and NAV questions in public vehicles, noting Oaktree’s limited direct lending and software exposure. He links private equity’s fortunes to direct lending and the end of ultra-low rates, and closes with parallels to past credit cycles.
key_points: Marks frames credit innovation as a chronology: high yield, LBOs, syndicated loans, securitization, alternatives, direct lending, and retail direct lending vehicles.
He says direct lending followed the classic pattern of early rewards, capital inflows, competition, lower yields and weaker protections, and managers mostly untested through a downturn.
Software debt is prominent in direct lending, with higher leverage and ARR loans; AI developments triggered scrutiny and volatility in private credit markets.
Redemption limits in semi-liquid vehicles have worked as designed so far, but investors may react negatively to being unable to withdraw when they want.
Oaktree says its direct lending and software exposures are limited, and it did not pursue direct lending to the same extent as others.
Private equity and direct lending are intertwined; higher rates have pressured portfolio companies, coverage ratios, exits, distributions, and LP commitments.

quotes.point: Signals the memo’s view that direct lending is entering a more testing phase.
quotes.text: the tide has begun to go out for direct lending

quotes.point: Warns that low reported volatility does not mean lower underlying credit risk.
quotes.text: Direct loans embody no less credit risk than liquid credit instruments

quotes.point: Summarizes Marks’s argument for discipline over chasing popular credit strategies.
quotes.text: Staying disciplined and resisting the latest fads isn’t the route to short-term maximization

implications.text: Distinguish private credit from direct lending and treat low reported volatility in private loans as not equivalent to low credit risk.
Review any direct lending, BDC, semi-liquid vehicle, or software-related credit exposure for redemption terms, NAV assumptions, leverage, and software concentration.
Track private credit and private equity stress as part of the broader credit cycle, especially refinancing, coverage ratios, exits, and distributions.
Remember the memo’s discipline argument: resist fads and do not assume recent direct lending success will persist without a credit cycle.
No Indonesia-specific claim appears in the memo; use it as a global credit-sentiment input rather than a direct IDR catalyst.

digests.author: Howard Marks (Oaktree Capital Management)
digests.title: AI Hurtles Ahead
digests.summary: Howard Marks frames this memo as an addendum to his December 9 memo, Is It a Bubble?, drawing heavily on a Claude-generated tutorial he commissioned and quotes liberally. He explains AI as a trained reasoning system (not a search engine) that is prompted by users, and recounts Claude's own argument that pattern-based synthesis is not structurally different from how an educated human mind works. The memo's core claim is that the pace and nature of AI change are unprecedented: adoption has reached roughly 400 million individuals and 75-80% of companies in about two years, and AI has moved from 'Chat AI' (Level 1) through tool use (Level 2) to autonomous agents (Level 3) that do work rather than assist it, with vendors reporting AI used to build AI. Marks accepts the technology is real and probably underestimated, and that inference capex is responding to actual demand, but distinguishes that from whether AI assets are fairly priced: infrastructure rushes have historically destroyed capital, some AI revenue is circular, and valuations of startups resemble lottery tickets. He keeps his prior advice of a moderate, selective position, and closes with a post-script on job losses and AI's speed outpacing society's ability to adjust.
key_points: Marks treats AI as a genuine, rapidly applied technology whose potential is 'more likely to be underestimated today' than exaggerated, but insists that is not the same as saying AI investments are fairly or cheaply priced.

He distinguishes training capex (speculative, built ahead of demand) from inference capex (a response to actual, growing demand), while noting Claude's supply-shortage argument ignores the infrastructure already in the pipeline.

The shift from Level 2 tool-using AI to Level 3 autonomous agents is presented as the decisive change: labor replacement at the task level rather than assistance, described as separating a $50 billion market from a multi-trillion-dollar one.

Marks weighs AI as an investor: it is fast, unemotional, unanchored and unbounded by fear or greed, but weak in genuinely novel situations, qualitative judgement, counterparty selection, and it has no skin in the game.
Some AI revenue is 'circular' — AI companies buying from each other — and how much must ultimately rest on end users paying for real economic value remains an open question.

On bubbles his answer is multi-part: the technology is real; application is real; the infrastructure rush will likely malinvest capital as in past innovations; returns on that spend can only be judged in about ten years; hyperscaler prices are unlikely to prove ruinous, listed pure-plays are untested, and multi-billion-dollar startups are 'lottery tickets'.

The post-script warns of large-scale displacement of knowledge work, compounded by AI's speed of adoption outrunning society's ability to retrain, and Marks remains unconvinced that new jobs will materialise.

quotes.point: Marks's actionable bottom line: size AI exposure for survivability rather than conviction, since bubble status cannot be determined definitively.
quotes.text: no one should go all-in without acknowledging that they face the risk of ruin if things go badly

quotes.point: A concrete test for AI-linked earnings quality: revenue between AI companies is not proof of end-user economic demand.
quotes.text: the question of how much revenue is circular remains an open one

quotes.point: Frames the investment case as labor substitution rather than productivity software, with a much larger addressable market and a direct earnings threat to labor-heavy business models.
quotes.text: Level 3 agents are the automobile. They don't make the work faster. They do the work.

implications.text: Keep AI exposure moderate and selective per Marks's advice; distinguish proven cash-generative hyperscalers from pre-revenue pure plays and note that the memo calls the latter 'lottery tickets'. Do not treat the demand-growth argument as a valuation argument.

Add two checks to the AI book: (1) how much of AI-linked revenue is circular between AI companies rather than end-user paid, and (2) the pipeline of announced infrastructure build-out, since Claude's supply-shortage case ignores it.

Track AI adoption speed and labor-substitution evidence as a macro variable, including the memo's point that AI's pace of change may exceed society's ability to adjust; treat displaced knowledge work as a demand and policy risk channel.

When AI-generated research enters the process, require a reasonableness check: the memo notes AI is weaker on genuinely unprecedented situations, can hallucinate confidence, has a limited context window, and carries an explicit 'double check responses' warning.

Review holdings with labor-heavy, structured-analytical cost bases (software, legal, consulting-type models) for substitution risk, and remember Marks's claim that readily available quantitative information no longer offers an edge that AI cannot match.

digests.author: Howard Marks
digests.title: Is It a Bubble?
digests.summary: Howard Marks’s December 9, 2025 memo asks whether AI is a bubble. He separates a possible bubble in AI companies’ behavior from a bubble in investor behavior, and says he cannot judge the former, so focuses on financial markets. Bubbles, he argues, are not caused directly by technology but by excessive optimism applied to new developments; newness removes historical limits on imagination. Citing Hobart and Huber, he distinguishes “mean-reversion bubbles” that destroy wealth from “inflection bubbles” tied to transformative technology, which can accelerate progress yet still destroy investors’ wealth. He sees today’s behavior as speculative: AI stocks dominate S&P gains, capex is large, and there are $1 billion seed rounds, circular deals, SPVs, and increasing debt. AI differs from past booms because products, users, revenues and strong incumbents already exist, and major AI p/e ratios are below those of 1998-2000 leaders. But enormous unknowns remain about winners, profits, asset life, demand and financing. Marks concludes no one can definitively say it is a bubble; bubbles are best identified in retrospect. He advises neither all-in nor all-out, but a moderate, selective, prudent position.
key_points: Marks separates bubbles in company behavior from bubbles in investor behavior, and focuses mainly on whether there is a financial-market bubble around AI.
Bubbles result from excessive optimism applied to new technological or financial developments, not directly from the developments themselves.
Hobart and Huber’s “inflection bubbles” can accelerate technological progress and still destroy wealth for many investors; “mean-reversion bubbles” merely rise and fall.
Today’s AI landscape shows speculative signs: enormous capex, $1 billion seed rounds, circular deals, SPVs and increasing debt financing.
AI has existing products, users, revenues and strong incumbents, and major AI p/e ratios are described as below 1998-2000 leaders, but winners, profits, asset life and demand remain highly uncertain.
Debt magnifies losses, increases failure probability and puts lenders at risk; Marks says debt is acceptable where outcomes are uncertain but not where they are pure conjecture.
Marks cannot definitively call a bubble; he says bubbles are best identified in retrospect and recommends a moderate, selective, prudent position.

quotes.point: Supports avoiding a definitive bubble call and focusing on risk posture rather than timing.
quotes.text: Bubbles are best identified in retrospect.

quotes.point: States Marks’s practical conclusion for investors facing AI uncertainty.
quotes.text: A moderate position, applied with selectivity and prudence, seems like the best approach.

quotes.point: Frames the memo’s debt discipline test: uncertain is acceptable, pure conjecture is not.
quotes.text: It’s okay to supply debt financing for a venture where the outcome is uncertain.

implications.text: Review AI and data-center exposure for concentration, circular counterparties, SPV or off-balance-sheet leverage, and asset-obsolescence assumptions.
Avoid all-in or all-out AI positioning; keep exposure moderate and selective, and distinguish equity participation in winner-take-most outcomes from debt exposure.
Use Marks’s framework to separate company-level speculation from investor psychology, and document bubble criteria rather than relying on labels.
Remember that the memo offers no definitive bubble verdict; monitor whether enthusiasm becomes irrational without claiming retrospective certainty.
Treat the memo as US AI-market analysis; do not map its conclusions to the Indonesia book without local evidence.

digests.author: Howard Marks
digests.title: Cockroaches in the Coal Mine
digests.summary: Howard Marks’s November 6, 2025 memo examines recent sub-investment-grade credit stress after bankruptcies at First Brands and Tricolor and subsequent bank disclosures. He notes allegations of fraud and repeated use of receivables as collateral, while cautioning that defaults are a normal part of sub-investment-grade investing—more than 2% of high-yield bonds by value have defaulted in a typical year over his 47 years. Marks says the episodes are not necessarily the beginning of a trend and are not an indictment of all private credit or sub-investment-grade debt; spreads exist because credit risk exists. He frames the issue through the cycle in attitudes toward risk: good times produce complacency, lower lending standards, and fertile conditions for fraud—Galbraith’s “bezzle”—while bad times expose malinvestment. First Brands illustrates red flags including opaque structures and extensive off-balance-sheet financing. Marks concludes that today’s issues are not “systemic” but “systematic,” that the last 16 good years may produce more credit surprises, and that renewed lender prudence would be positive.
key_points: First Brands and Tricolor bankruptcies, plus bank disclosures, focused attention on sub-investment-grade and private credit credit risk.
Marks says defaults are normal and the episodes are not necessarily the start of a trend or an indictment of the whole market.
He describes a cycle in risk attitudes: good times lower standards, encourage carelessness, and create conditions for fraud.
Galbraith’s “bezzle” explains how fraudulently inflated wealth grows in good times and shrinks when scrutiny returns.
First Brands showed red flags including opaque structures, aggressive off-balance-sheet financing, and receivables issues.
Marks calls the issues “systematic” rather than “systemic,” while warning that 16 good years may produce more credit surprises.
He stresses prudence, second-level credit analysis, early detection, and the liquidity advantage of public debt.

quotes.point: Dimon’s warning frames credit failures as a possible cluster rather than isolated events.
quotes.text: when you see one cockroach, there are probably more

quotes.point: It links benign periods to weakened lending standards and later credit losses.
quotes.text: The worst of loans are made in the best of times.

quotes.point: Marks limits the systemic-contagion reading while still calling the pattern systematic.
quotes.text: I don’t think today’s issues are systemic

implications.text: Treat recent credit failures as a reminder of clustered credit risk; monitor sub-investment-grade and private-credit exposures for fraud/default indicators without assuming systemic contagion, since Marks calls the issues systematic, not systemic.

Review North credit holdings for private-credit liquidity mismatch and the First Brands red flags—opaque structures, extensive off-balance-sheet financing, receivables factoring, weak controls—and favor public debt where exit liquidity matters, all else equal.
Balance deploying capital with prudence; require credit analysis to be a mosaic of inferences and act early on negative conclusions rather than waiting for market consensus.

Remember defaults are normal and spreads compensate credit risk; do not extrapolate one or two bankruptcies into a broad sub-investment-grade or private-credit thesis, but note Marks’s view that 16 good years may yield more credit surprises.
No Indonesia-specific claim appears in the memo; do not mechanically map US private-credit episodes to the South book, but keep South credit underwriting standards and fraud checks explicit.

digests.author: Howard Marks
digests.title: A Look Under the Hood
digests.summary: Howard Marks recounts a consultant’s presentation to a U.S. state pension fund board, based on a board-member survey, and offers his reactions. He praises a two-by-two matrix separating the plan’s financial ability to bear risk from its willingness to do so, with cells labeled capitalizing, defensive, protective, and naive. The board had above-average ability but moderate willingness, implying constrained returns and a narrower range of outcomes. Marks agrees with the board’s objective ranking, which puts beating peers last, and argues that a defined benefit plan’s success is paying benefits and minimizing sponsor cost, not outperforming others. He distinguishes volatility from permanent loss, while acknowledging volatility can matter for pension contributions and endowment draws. On approach, the board favors preparing for all environments, accepts 15–20% leverage, and a slimmer majority backs 25% illiquidity if obligations can be met. Marks says performance should ultimately be judged against the actuarial assumption, but short-term assessment is necessarily relative and flawed; a full market cycle is needed to distinguish skill from risk bias. He also flags personnel turnover as a diagnostic.
key_points: Marks praises a risk matrix that separates a plan’s financial ability to bear risk from its willingness to bear risk, labeling the four cells capitalizing, defensive, protective, and naive.
The surveyed board had above-average ability to bear risk but only moderate willingness, which the consultant said would constrain returns while limiting the range of outcomes.
Board members ranked beating peers last among objectives and strongly disagreed that losing money when others do is acceptable if you do well when others do.
Marks argues volatility is not the same as permanent loss, though volatility can be a legitimate concern for pension funds and endowments because of contributions and draws.
The board favored preparing for all environments, accepted leverage at 15–20% of assets, and a slimmer majority backed 25% in illiquid assets if benefit payments and funding requirements can be met.

Marks says long-term success should be measured against the actuarial assumption, but short-term assessment is necessarily relative and imperfect; a full market cycle is needed to distinguish skill from risk bias.
Marks flags personnel turnover as a possible signal of hiring, assessment, or management problems, while noting some turnover is understandable.

quotes.point: Marks distinguishes volatility from permanent loss, a key risk framework for the desk.
quotes.text: in pure investment terms, there’s no intrinsic reason for long-term investors to be concerned with volatility

quotes.point: Supports judging investment skill over a full market cycle rather than a single environment.
quotes.text: an appropriate performance assessment period has to include both good times and bad

quotes.point: Frames objectives around liabilities and sponsor cost, not peer ranking.
quotes.text: Success for a defined benefit pension plan means being able to pay benefits and minimize the cost to the plan sponsor. Period.

implications.text: Use the ability-versus-willingness risk matrix explicitly when framing portfolio risk capacity; the memo treats this as a core governance decision.
Avoid treating peer outperformance in a bull market as proof of skill; the memo says a full cycle including good and bad times is needed to distinguish skill from risk bias.
Do not directly import the U.S. pension plan’s leverage and illiquidity conclusions; the memo describes positions for a specific well-funded plan with a strong sponsor.
Separate volatility from permanent loss in risk reporting, while recognizing that volatility can be a real constraint for investors with contribution or draw needs.
When assessing performance, remember the memo’s warning that short-term relative standards are flawed and that the assessment period should cover both good and bad markets.

digests.author: Howard Marks
digests.title: The Best of . . .
digests.summary: Howard Marks marks 35 years of his memos by releasing a collection of the ones he considers best. He groups them into two categories: memos setting out enduring truths of investing—second-level thinking, risk control, the inevitability of cycles, and the futility of macro forecasting—and memos chronicling major financial events, including the dot-com bubble, the Global Financial Crisis, and the 2022 sea change in interest-rate policy. The collection spans his first memo, The Route to Performance (1990), which argued for consistently good returns and an absence of poor years rather than occasional brilliance, through later pieces on market efficiency, the “I don’t know” school, risk as more than volatility, too much eager capital, the “all-good trilogy” warnings before the GFC, leverage and volatility, luck versus skill, uncertainty, asymmetry, fewer losers in credit, and the relationship between value and price. Marks says writing the memos is a joy, a way to share his thinking with the investment community and connect with Oaktree’s clients and employees, and he plans to keep at it.
key_points: Marks released a collection of memos he considers the best to celebrate 35 years of writing them.
The memos fall mainly into two groups: enduring investing truths and major financial events such as the dot-com bubble, the Global Financial Crisis, and the 2022 rate sea change.
Recurring principles include second-level thinking, risk control, the inevitability of cycles, and the futility of macro forecasting.
The first memo, The Route to Performance, argued for long-term success through consistently good returns and an absence of poor years rather than occasional brilliance.
Several memos warn about too much eager capital, excessive leverage, easy credit, and swings in investor psychology.
Later memos emphasize uncertainty, luck versus skill, asymmetry, fewer losers in credit, and the relationship between value and price.

quotes.point: Marks favors understanding the current environment over relying on macro forecasts.
quotes.text: we may never know where we’re going, but we ought to know where we are

quotes.point: This is Oaktree’s stated motto and reflects its risk-control orientation.
quotes.text: if we avoid the losers, the winners will take care of themselves.

quotes.point: Marks ties future performance to the current relationship of price to value.
quotes.text: high valuations presaging low subsequent returns, and vice versa.

implications.text: Do not build the desk’s process around macro forecasts; Marks repeatedly argues they are seldom helpful and that knowing today’s environment matters more.
Treat risk as a range of possible outcomes rather than volatility, and check leverage against asset volatility and the holder’s staying power.
Favor consistent, risk-controlled return profiles and avoidance of poor years over swinging for occasional brilliance; in credit, fewer losers generally serves best.
When the investing environment changes fundamentally, review strategy thoroughly; the memo cites the 2022 rate sea change as such a case.
Evaluate managers on long records of consistent, possibly modest outperformance rather than occasional flashes of brilliance.

digests.author: Howard Marks (Oaktree Capital Management)
digests.title: The Calculus of Value
digests.summary: Marks uses this memo to lay out how he thinks investment value is derived and how price relates to it, then applies that framework to U.S. markets as of mid-2025. Value comes from fundamentals — ultimately an asset's earning power, present and prospective; price is the consensus of investors' subjective opinions, and because investor psychology swings between flawless and hopeless, price fluctuates far more than value and can overshoot in either direction. Price only acts as a 'magnetic' pull toward value over the long run, not on any timetable. Applying this, he notes the S&P 500 entered 2025 highly valued (forward p/e around 23), fell up to 15% after the April 2 tariff announcement, then rallied 29% from its April 8 low to sit 9% higher year-to-date. Fundamentals look somewhat worse than seven months ago — tariff-driven inflation risk, fewer expected rate cuts, fiscal deficits, doubts about U.S. reliability as a partner — while prices are higher and valuation metrics (price/sales at an all-time high, market cap/GDP at a record, thin credit yield spreads) look stretched. He concludes the market has gone from 'elevated' to 'worrisome' and favors greater defensiveness, with credit as a defensive holding.
key_points: Value derives from fundamentals — ultimately earning power, current and prospective; assets without earning power (gold, art, collectibles) cannot be valued analytically.
Price is set by investors' subjective opinions; swings in psychology make price far more volatile than value, creating the bargains and overpricings the Efficient Market Hypothesis denies.
Price should be expected to converge toward value, but only in the long run — Keynes's warning that the market can remain irrational longer than you can remain solvent.
The S&P 500's forward p/e was around 23 at end-2024; it fell up to 15% below year-end levels after the April 2 tariffs, then rallied 29% off the April 8 low to be up 9% year-to-date.

Valuation indicators are stretched: price/sales above 3.3x (an all-time high per FT/Bloomberg), market cap/GDP at a record, a Barclays 'equity-euphoria indicator' at twice normal, and credit yield spreads near all-time lows.
The Magnificent Seven average a p/e of roughly 33 and are one-third of the index's market value; Marks finds the 493 other companies' average p/e of 22 more worrisome.
He moves the market from 'elevated' to 'worrisome' and endorses INVESTCON 5 — stop buying and shift from aggressive to defensive holdings — while calling INVESTCON 3, 2 and 1 effectively unreachable.
Credit is presented as the natural defensive holding: narrower spreads mean less generous relative returns, but absolute yields are significant and backed by contractual promises.

quotes.point: The memo's central verdict — a downgrade of the U.S. equity outlook, not a crash call.
quotes.text: taken together, they tell me the stock market has moved from “elevated” to “worrisome.”

quotes.point: Concrete action guidance: stop buying and rotate from aggressive to defensive holdings.
quotes.text: But I have no problem thinking it’s time for INVESTCON 5.

quotes.point: Directs where the defensiveness should be expressed — credit rather than equities.
quotes.text: credit investments are generally more secure than stocks, and thus well suited to serve as defensive holdings

implications.text: Treat this as a de-risking prompt rather than a sell signal: the memo explicitly says overvaluation never means 'sure to go down soon.' Consider an INVESTCON 5 posture — pause new aggressive additions and tilt the book toward defensive holdings.

Review U.S. equity exposure against the specific markers cited: forward p/e ~23 at end-2024, price/sales above 3.3x, market cap/GDP at a record, and a 493-stock average p/e of 22. Check how much of North's return depends on the Magnificent Seven (about one-third of index market value).

Log the memo's crowding indicators — the Barclays 'equity-euphoria indicator' at twice normal, meme-stock attention, and credit yield spreads near all-time lows — as evidence of elevated risk tolerance, and note that many current investors have never worked through a prolonged bear market.

The memo does not analyse Indonesia; do not extrapolate. Use it only as a sentiment input, and note the caveat that thin credit spreads mean credit's prospective returns are less generous relative to risk-free assets than in history.

Remember the memo's own hedge: 'it's different this time' is usually a bull-market cliché but occasionally true, and Marks says he does not know which applies to AI today. Do not let a valuation-based caution harden into a timing conviction.

digests.author: Howard Marks (Oaktree Capital Management)
digests.title: More on Repealing the Laws of Economics
digests.summary: Howard Marks revisits his September memo arguing that economies operate under laws such as supply and demand and incentives, and that governments sometimes try to override them. He cites rent control, where capping rents reduces landlord investment, new construction and tenant mobility, and California fire insurance, where regulators limited premiums and barred forward-looking catastrophe models; insurers withdrew, and by the time of the 2025 wildfires fewer than a quarter of affected properties were insured, including a dozen Oaktree employees who lost homes. He then turns to tariffs, describing them as a tax that protects domestic producers and workers at the expense of domestic consumers and global welfare, and argues the decline of U.S. manufacturing largely reflects rising incomes rather than unfair trade, citing Niall Ferguson. Targeted tariffs for national security, iconic industries or unfair practices may be defensible, but taxing all goods from all countries is different. Finally he flags U.S. fiscal deficits and Social Security trust fund exhaustion projected for 2035, with neither party willing to act. Free markets produce imperfect solutions, but efforts to significantly control them make things worse.
key_points: Governments can cap prices but cannot compel supply: rent control discourages landlords, developers and mobility, and premium caps cannot make insurers write policies.

California insurers were barred from using forward-looking catastrophe models and from passing through reinsurance costs; Chubb, Allstate and State Farm withdrew or stopped writing, and fewer than a quarter of affected properties were insured at the time of the 2025 fires.
Marks calls tariffs a tax: the exporter, exporting country or importer may absorb part, otherwise the end-consumer pays via price increases.
He distinguishes targeted tariffs (national security, iconic industries, unfair trade practices) from taxing all goods from all countries.

Citing Niall Ferguson, he argues manufacturing's employment share declines in every developed economy as per-capita GDP rises; U.S. manufacturing is now about 8% of non-farm jobs versus roughly 30% in 1950, with about 400,000 openings.
U.S. deficits occurred in 41 of the last 45 years and the FY2024 deficit was roughly $1.8 trillion, or 6.4% of GDP, in a time of prosperity; annual interest cost already exceeds defense spending.
Social Security Trust Funds are projected to be exhausted in 2035, at which point receipts would cover only an estimated 79% of promised benefits absent corrective action.

quotes.point: The memo's core mechanism: price caps suppress supply rather than deliver affordability, leaving buyers with less access.
quotes.text: you can limit the price insurers can charge for coverage, but you can't make them provide coverage at that price

quotes.point: Frames tariffs and regulation as costs shifted to consumers, not free wins — relevant when reading policy headlines.
quotes.text: That's a tradeoff – the kind of thing free markets require and leaders who would mandate economic outcomes would prefer to ignore.

quotes.point: Buffett quote Marks endorses on the U.S. fiscal path, tying deficits to eventual limits on credit and low rates.
quotes.text: We're operating at a fiscal deficit now that is unsustainable over a very long period of time.

implications.text: Log the memo's fiscal points as a long-horizon, not near-term, framework: deficits in 41 of 45 years, $1.8 trillion / 6.4% of GDP in FY2024, interest above defense, and Social Security exhaustion projected for 2035. Do not convert these into a timing signal.

When assessing tariff-driven inflation, use Marks's distinction between targeted and broad tariffs and his point that domestic producers may raise prices under the umbrella of higher import prices — check whether such increases are appearing rather than assuming tariffs are absorbed abroad.

The California insurance case is a supply-withdrawal lesson: regulation that caps price without allowing forward-looking risk pricing led to insurer exits and a concentrated state-backed FAIR Plan, with solvency concerns noted. Flag any book exposure where price is set below risk and supply can leave.
The memo does not discuss Indonesia or the South book. Treat the tariff and price-control arguments as general framework only; no South-specific action follows from this document.

Record the memo's own conclusion — free markets produce imperfect outcomes but efforts to significantly control them make things worse — as a philosophical input, not an asset-price view; stance is n/a.

digests.author: Howard Marks
digests.title: Nobody Knows (Yet Again)
digests.summary: Howard Marks’s April 9, 2025 memo reuses the title of his post-Lehman and Covid memos to argue that the tariff shock is another moment when nobody knows the future. He says the future cannot be “analyzed”; forecasts need a probability of being right, and under current unprecedented unknowns they are even less reliable than usual. Trump’s tariff increases were larger than markets anticipated, and Marks says all norms have been overthrown. He lists tariff goals but stresses second- and third-order consequences: retaliation, higher prices and inflation, demand destruction, recession and lost jobs, supply shortages, and a changed world order. Tariffs are taxes on imports, usually passed to consumers; restoring U.S. manufacturing faces capacity, construction-time, skilled-labor and cost constraints. He defends globalization and comparative advantage, and worries that antagonizing partners could reduce foreign demand for Treasurys amid a $36 trillion national debt. His bottom line calls the tariffs an “own goal” analogous to Brexit, likely bringing recession sooner, higher inflation and dislocation; even reversal may not restore trust. He says the Fed’s response is unknowable. Oaktree sees higher credit yields and expects to invest its opportunistic debt fund faster, while Marks says it is appropriate to look for bargains.
key_points: Marks reuses “Nobody Knows” because the tariff shock lacks applicable facts or prior experience; forecasts are less likely to be correct and must include a probability of being right.
He calls the tariff developments an “own goal” analogous to Brexit, with negative effects likely felt immediately while hoped-for gains would come only after a multi-year adjustment.
Tariffs are taxes on imports and are usually passed to consumers; listed likely consequences include retaliation, inflation, demand destruction, recession, shortages and a changed world order.
He questions restoring U.S. manufacturing because of insufficient capacity, long construction timelines, skilled-labor constraints and higher absolute prices.
He defends globalization and comparative advantage, and worries that antagonizing partners could reduce foreign demand for U.S. Treasurys amid the $36 trillion national debt.
Marks says the Fed’s response is unknowable: recession might call for rate cuts, while inflation might delay them, and tariff-driven inflation may respond less to higher rates.
Oaktree sees higher yield spreads and expects to invest its latest opportunistic debt fund faster; Marks says inaction is itself an act and it is appropriate to look for bargains.

quotes.point: Marks frames the tariff shock as an epistemic problem, not a forecastable event.
quotes.text: Truly nobody knows, and a lot of this memo will be about things we can’t know for sure.

quotes.point: This is his bottom-line judgment that the policy is self-inflicted damage.
quotes.text: I consider the tariff developments thus far to be what soccer fans call an “own goal”

quotes.point: Despite macro caution, he sees reason to look for credit bargains.
quotes.text: Now, with heretofore unimaginable risks on the table and priced in, it’s appropriate to sniff around for bargains

implications.text: Treat the tariff path as unknowable rather than forecastable; build scenarios for retaliation/escalation versus rollback, remembering that negative effects are likely immediate while gains are long-run.

Review USD book exposure to import-cost inflation, demand destruction, recession risk and Treasury/dollar funding assumptions; the memo questions continued foreign demand for Treasurys but reaches no conclusion.
The memo contains no Indonesia-specific analysis; do not infer one. Check only verified internal exposures to global trade disruption, USD funding and risk-off credit spreads.
Scrutinize no-action as an active decision; require probability confidence around any forecast and stress liquidity and credit-spread marks against higher default fear and wider spreads.
Avoid certainty; if acting on credit bargains, stage entries and document rationale, consistent with Marks’s view that inaction must be judged like action.

digests.author: Howard Marks
digests.title: Gimme Credit
digests.summary: Howard Marks’s March 6, 2025 memo focuses on credit, especially high yield bonds, after two strong years: the ICE BofA US High Yield Index returned 13.5% in 2023 and 8.2% in 2024, or 10.8% annualized over 2023-24. He notes the average high yield yield-to-maturity has fallen from about 9½% in 2022 to just above 7%, and the spread is around 290 bps, among the narrowest since high yield issuance began in 1977-78. Marks argues the key question is whether today’s spread offsets likely credit losses, not whether it is historically narrow. Historical high yield defaults averaged 3.5% and losses about 230 bps, though he cites caveats: the average overstates the typical year, median defaults were 2.7%, and the universe’s ratings have improved. He also says buying at the 2007 all-time tight spread still produced strong 10- and 15-year returns. Because bond returns are contractual, interim spread widening is temporary if issuers pay. On private credit, he sees higher yields but illiquidity, no marking to market, higher fees, and untested manager behavior; he does not see systemic risk and suggests combining public and private credit. He concludes credit offers a better deal than equities even at today’s spreads.
key_points: High yield returned 13.5% in 2023 and 8.2% in 2024; 10.8% annualized over 2023-24.
Average high yield yield-to-maturity fell from about 9.5% in 2022 to just above 7%; spread is around 290 bps, among the narrowest since 1977-78.
Marks says adequacy depends on offsetting credit losses; historical default average was 3.5%, median 2.7%, and annual credit losses about 230 bps.
Caveats include crisis years overstating the average default rate and an improved ratings profile, with BB at 52.6% at end-2024 versus 32.7% in 1999.
Buying at the June 2007 all-time tight spread still outperformed Treasurys and the Aggregate over 10 and 15 years; narrow spreads are not synonymous with sub-par medium-to-long-term performance.

Private credit offers higher yields and leverage but has illiquidity, no mark-to-market, higher fees, and untested manager behavior; Marks does not see it as systemic and suggests combining public and private credit.
Credit offers a better deal than equities even at today’s spreads; Marks prefers higher yields and wider spreads but says that preference is not a reason not to increase credit allocations today.

quotes.point: Emphasizes that total return, not the spread level alone, is what ultimately matters.
quotes.text: you can’t eat spread, or spend spread, or pay pension benefits with spread

quotes.point: Supports a constructive stance on credit despite historically narrow spreads.
quotes.text: Credit isn’t a giveaway today, but it offers healthy absolute returns and is fairly priced in relative terms.

quotes.point: Balances the case for private credit against its liquidity and management drawbacks.
quotes.text: the return premium on private credit relative to public credit seems roughly fair given the merits

implications.text: Track whether high yield spreads near 290 bps remain adequate to offset default losses; the memo’s key test is total return, not historical spread levels.
Review credit allocations across high yield, senior loans, mezzanine, asset-backed loans, CLOs and private lending; the author favors increasing credit and combining public and private exposure.
Do not infer an IDR or Indonesia credit view from this USD-focused memo; treat it as a global credit framework and require separate local analysis.
Monitor private credit managers for relaxed credit standards, mark-to-market limitations, forbearance and possible leverage layers; the memo says flaws may appear only when the tide goes out.
Remember narrow spreads are not synonymous with sub-par medium-to-long-term performance; hold-to-maturity contractual returns can offset temporary spread widening.
Weigh credit against equities on expected total return and contractual certainty, not only on whether spreads are historically tight.

digests.author: Warren E. Buffett
digests.title: Berkshire Hathaway Inc. — To the Shareholders
digests.summary: Warren Buffett’s February 22, 2025 shareholder letter reviews Berkshire’s 2024 results and long-term principles. Operating earnings were $47.4 billion, helped by higher Treasury Bill yields and a major GEICO improvement, even though 53% of the 189 operating businesses reported lower earnings. Marketable equity holdings fell to $272 billion from $354 billion, but Buffett says the great majority of Berkshire money remains in equities and that cash-equivalent assets will never be preferred over good businesses. P/C insurance remains core: float reached $171 billion, pricing strengthened after convective-storm damage, and Buffett warns that a truly staggering loss will occur someday. Berkshire paid $26.8 billion to the IRS, about 5% of corporate America’s total, reflecting decades of reinvestment and only one dividend. The letter discusses mistakes and the need to correct them, praises Pete Liegl, details the five Japanese trading-house holdings and yen-balanced borrowings, and says Greg Abel will soon replace Buffett as CEO and write the annual letters.
key_points: 2024 operating earnings were $47.4 billion versus $37.35 billion in 2023, aided by investment income and GEICO, though 53% of 189 operating businesses reported declining earnings.

Marketable equity holdings fell to $272 billion from $354 billion; Buffett says the great majority of Berkshire money remains in equities and cash-equivalent assets will never be preferred over good businesses.
P/C insurance remains Berkshire’s core business; float reached $171 billion, pricing strengthened after convective-storm damage, and Berkshire must shrink when prices are inadequate.
Berkshire paid $26.8 billion to the U.S. Treasury, about 5% of all corporate America paid, reflecting a history of reinvestment and only one cash dividend since 1965.

Berkshire’s five Japanese trading-house holdings cost $13.8 billion and were worth $23.5 billion at yearend; expected 2025 dividends are about $812 million versus about $135 million of yen-debt interest cost.
Buffett, 94, says Greg Abel will soon replace him as CEO and write the annual letters; Buffett also discusses mistakes and the need to correct them without delay.

quotes.point: Relevant to portfolio reviews and governance: errors should be corrected promptly rather than tolerated.
quotes.text: The cardinal sin is delaying the correction of mistakes or what Charlie Munger called “thumb-sucking.”

quotes.point: Signals a durable equity bias despite commentary about Berkshire’s cash position.
quotes.text: Berkshire will never prefer ownership of cash-equivalent assets over the ownership of good businesses, whether controlled or only partially owned.

quotes.point: Highlights underwriting discipline and the risk of writing business for volume rather than price.
quotes.text: We must never write inadequately-priced policies in order to stay in the game.

implications.text: Remember Buffett’s warning that paper money can lose value if fiscal folly prevails and that fixed-coupon bonds provide no protection against runaway currency; monitor currency and fiscal risk accordingly.
Use the letter’s stated preference for good businesses over cash-equivalent assets as a reminder not to over-weight cash solely because Berkshire’s cash position draws commentary.
Check insurance-like exposures for long-tail loss risk and pricing discipline; the document says Berkshire must never write inadequately-priced policies to stay in the game.
Note the imminent CEO succession to Greg Abel; the document says Abel shares Berkshire’s creed that a report is owed to owners and warns against fooling shareholders.

Remember the Japan holdings are described as very long term and supported by fixed-rate yen borrowings intended to approximate currency-neutrality; 2025 expected dividend income is about $812 million versus about $135 million interest cost.

digests.author: Howard Marks
digests.title: On Bubble Watch
digests.summary: Howard Marks revisits bubbles 25 years after his bubble.com memo. He argues a bubble is more a state of mind than a quantitative calculation, marked by irrational exuberance, adoration of the subject companies, fear of missing out, and belief that there is no price too high. Newness and “this time is different” remove historical tethers. He recalls the Nifty Fifty and TMT bubble and states guiding principles: what you pay matters, good investing means buying things well, and no asset is so good it cannot become overpriced. He notes the Magnificent Seven were 32–33% of S&P 500 capitalization at end-October, roughly double five years earlier and above the roughly 22% top-seven share in 2000; U.S. stocks were over 70% of the MSCI World Index at end-November, highest since 1970. Today’s leaders are strong, and Nvidia’s multiple is in the low 30s, but persistence is hard. Cautionary signs include optimism since late 2022, above-average S&P valuation, AI enthusiasm, presumption the top seven will continue, and possible automated index buying. Counterarguments include a high but not insane p/e and incredible companies. He cites a J.P. Morgan chart linking starting valuations to subsequent ten-year returns and does not authoritatively call a bubble.
key_points: Marks defines bubbles primarily through psychology—irrational exuberance, adoration, FOMO, and ‘no price too high’—rather than only valuation.
He says newness and ‘this time is different’ remove historical valuation tethers; every mania usually has a grain of truth but gets taken too far.

The Magnificent Seven were 32–33% of S&P 500 capitalization at end-October, roughly double five years earlier and above the roughly 22% top-seven share in 2000; U.S. stocks were over 70% of MSCI World at end-November, highest since 1970.

Persistence is hard: only six of the top twenty S&P 500 companies at the beginning of 2000 were still top twenty at the beginning of 2024; only Microsoft among today’s Magnificent Seven was in the top twenty 24 years earlier.

Cautionary signs today include optimism since late 2022, above-average S&P valuation, AI enthusiasm, presumption the top seven continue, possible automated index buying, and Bitcoin’s 465% two-year rise.

Counterarguments are that the S&P p/e is high but not insane, the Magnificent Seven are incredible companies, he does not hear ‘no price too high,’ and markets do not seem nutty to him; he cannot authoritatively say whether it is a bubble.

A J.P. Morgan chart he cites shows higher starting valuations consistently lead to lower subsequent ten-year returns; at today’s p/e around 22, historical observations showed ten-year returns between plus 2% and minus 2%.

quotes.point: Frames bubble risk as psychological, so the desk should watch behavior and language, not only valuation.
quotes.text: But for me, a bubble or crash is more a state of mind than a quantitative calculation.

quotes.point: Supports treating AI enthusiasm as potentially real but overextended, not dismissible.
quotes.text: There’s usually a grain of truth that underlies every mania and bubble. It just gets taken too far.

quotes.point: Warns that popular market leaders can be vulnerable despite quality.
quotes.text: When something is on the pedestal of popularity, the risk of a decline is high.

implications.text: Use Marks’s psychological checklist—irrational exuberance, FOMO, ‘no price too high’—alongside valuation data to monitor global risk appetite; track S&P p/e, top-seven concentration, and AI enthusiasm as sentiment indicators.
Review USD book exposure to U.S. mega-cap concentration and any assumptions of leader persistence; the memo notes only Microsoft from today’s Magnificent Seven was in the top twenty 24 years earlier.

Flag concentration and bubble-thinking language as risk indicators; stress-test for multiple compression, remembering Marks cites historical ten-year returns of plus 2% to minus 2% when starting p/e was around today’s 22.
Present the memo as balanced, not a definitive bubble call: it lists cautionary signs and counterarguments and says Marks cannot speak authoritatively about whether a bubble exists.
The memo contains no Indonesia or IDR analysis; do not infer a direct South book action from it.

digests.author: Howard Marks (Oaktree Capital Management)
digests.title: Ruminating on Asset Allocation
digests.summary: Howard Marks uses client conversations in Australia to set out a unified view of asset allocation. He argues that, at bottom, there are only two asset classes — ownership and debt — and that they differ in kind, not degree: owners take risk with no promised return and share in residual profit, while lenders receive contractual, pre-known payments. Ownership assets generally offer higher expected returns with more upside and more downside; debt offers lower but tighter outcomes, so offense is usually played through ownership and defense through debt. The single most important portfolio decision, in his view, is the targeted risk posture — the balance between preserving capital and maximizing growth — and the goal should be optimization, not maximization, with absolute risk consciously targeted rather than left as a by-product. Marks notes that credit's expected return is now much closer to equities than in the 2009-21 low-rate era, citing roughly 7% on public credit and 10% on private credit, and recommends investors research and begin building a credit allocation, taking only a partial step now because better entry points may return.
key_points: Marks reduces asset allocation to two fundamental asset classes: ownership and debt, which are 'a difference in kind' rather than degree.
The most important decision in portfolio management is the targeted risk posture — the balance between aggressiveness and defensiveness — with all other choices described as implementation.
The goal should be optimization, not maximization: the absolute level of risk must be consciously targeted and well compensated, 'neither too much nor too little.'
The risk/return relationship is not the simple linear graph taught at Chicago; wider ranges of outcomes and worse bad outcomes accompany higher risk (no free lunch).
Market efficiency is overstated: markets may incorporate information rapidly but the resulting consensus price 'can be far from correct,' leaving room for alpha from skillful selection.
Non-investment-grade credit now offers roughly 7% public / 10% private returns, competitive with historical equity returns and more dependable because contractual.
His recommendation is research plus a credit 'program' and a partial implementation step, since higher credit returns existed a year or two earlier and could return if optimism fades.

quotes.point: Frames allocation as a binary ownership-versus-lending choice rather than a menu of many asset classes.
quotes.text: the essential choice is between (a) owning part of it and (b) making a loan to it

quotes.point: The core risk/return asymmetry that should drive the offense/defense mix.
quotes.text: Ownership assets typically have a higher expected return, greater upside potential, and greater downside risk

quotes.point: Actionable stance: build a credit program and implement partially, not fully.
quotes.text: My recommendation at this time is that investors do the research required to increase their allocation to credit

implications.text: Register Marks's 'sea change' rate thesis as the backdrop: credit expected returns are described as much higher than in 2009-21 and closer to equity returns.
Consider researching a credit allocation program in the USD book, with roughly 7% public / 10% private cited as the relevant return range, and implement only partially per his advice.
The memo contains no Indonesia or IDR-specific content; treat it as a global framework note and do not extrapolate the 7-10% credit yields to the South book without local data.
Check that the book's absolute risk level is a consciously targeted input to allocation rather than an unintended output of return-seeking, and that it sits 'neither too much nor too little.'
Remember the optimization-not-maximization framing: define the offense/defense balance first, then treat asset-class, geography and quality choices as implementation details.

digests.author: Howard Marks
digests.title: Shall We Repeal the Laws of Economics?
digests.summary: Howard Marks argues that many campaign and policy proposals ignore economic reality, illustrating with Trump’s tariff call and Harris’s attack on grocery profiteering. He says there is no free lunch: prices and outcomes reflect supply, demand, incentives and tradeoffs, and governments cannot mandate economic results without consequences. Marks examines price gouging, arguing it is hard to define and that many grocery price increases reflected pandemic demand, supply-chain disruption, stimulus and strong demand rather than simple malevolence. He cites failed price-control attempts, including WIN buttons and Venezuela, and rent control in New York as examples that reduce supply and investment and create shortages. He also discusses first-time homebuyer subsidies, broad tariffs, tax cuts and deficits, California wage mandates and Social Security insolvency. He calls U.S. deficits and debt an embarrassment and notes annual interest now exceeds the Defense Department budget. He contrasts free markets with command economies, credits China’s success partly to its private sector, and concludes that incentives and supply/demand cannot be ignored; economics offers tradeoffs, not limitless benefits.
key_points: Marks says campaign proposals such as Trump tariffs and Harris’s grocery-profiteering attack ignore costs or misdiagnose the problem; there is no free lunch in economics.

Price gouging is hard to define, and many grocery price increases reflected pandemic demand, supply-chain disruption, stimulus and strong demand; laws already cover collusion, price fixing and predatory pricing.
Price controls and rent control are presented as examples that blunt supply/demand, discourage supply and investment, and create shortages or vacancies.

Other policy examples include first-time homebuyer subsidies that could raise home prices, broad tariffs likely paid by consumers, tax cuts and deficits, California wage mandates, and Social Security insolvency.
Marks calls U.S. deficits and debt an embarrassment and says annual interest on the national debt exceeds the Defense Department budget.
China’s economic success is attributed partly to a vibrant private sector, described by the 60/70/80/90 formulation.
Free markets vs command economies: incentives direct capital and labor and encourage risk taking, but produce uneven outcomes and require tradeoffs.

quotes.point: Central thesis: policy promises cannot escape economic costs and tradeoffs.
quotes.text: there is no “free lunch” in economics, despite candidates’ assertions to the contrary.

quotes.point: Explains why price controls can cause shortages and reduced supply.
quotes.text: you can set prices for goods, but you can’t make people produce them.

quotes.point: Marks’s conclusion that attempts to override supply, demand and incentives face eventual consequences.
quotes.text: The laws of economics will always win out eventually.

implications.text: Track U.S. policy proposals on tariffs, price controls, housing subsidies and taxes as potential inflation, fiscal and supply-side risks; the memo argues they carry second-order costs.
Treat broad tariff and anti-gouging or rent-control proposals as possible consumer-price and regulatory pressures for U.S. exposures; no specific sectors or trades are named.
Remember that price controls and regulation can distort supply/demand and create shortages or reduced investment; monitor second-order consequences rather than headline intent.
The document does not analyse Indonesia or emerging markets; no direct South book action follows from it.
No direct trade or valuation signal is given; use the memo as background for policy-risk discussions rather than as a positioning recommendation.

digests.author: Howard Marks
digests.title: Mr. Market Miscalculates
digests.summary: Howard Marks uses Benjamin Graham’s Mr. Market metaphor to explain the rapid market decline and rebound in early August 2024. He recounts the backdrop: a 54% S&P 500 rise in the 21 months through July 31, 2024; the Bank of Japan’s largest short-term rate increase in over 17 years, to 0.25%, which disrupted the Japanese carry trade and forced levered positions to unwind; mixed U.S. data, including unemployment at 4.3% and the Sahm Rule; and Berkshire Hathaway’s Apple share sales. Marks calls this a triple whammy that flipped sentiment and drove a 6.1% S&P 500 fall over August 1, 2 and 5. He argues that prices often diverge from fair value because perception swings between “flawless” and “hopeless,” with cognitive dissonance, contagion, wishful thinking and short financial memory amplifying moves. Markets are a short-term voting machine, not a fundamental analyst. Investors should avoid irrational jags, form independent views of intrinsic value, and trade with Mr. Market when his prices are extreme.
key_points: Graham’s Mr. Market metaphor shows prices can diverge from fair value, and overreactions can create opportunities.

Early-August 2024: a BOJ rate hike to 0.25% disrupted the carry trade and levered positions; mixed U.S. data and Berkshire’s Apple sales formed a “triple whammy”; the S&P 500 fell 6.1% over August 1, 2 and 5 after a 54% rise.
Marks says perception swings from “flawless” to “hopeless”; mood, cognitive dissonance, contagion, wishful thinking and short memory drive volatility more than daily fundamentals.
Markets are short-term voting machines and poor fundamental analysts during crises; daily price moves mostly reflect psychology and who wants to own or un-own assets.
Investors should not join irrational jags; better to watch or accommodate Mr. Market by selling when he overpays and buying when he panics, based on analysis.

quotes.point: Frames the memo’s core claim that mood, not daily fundamentals, drives sharp price moves.
quotes.text: in investing, perception often swings from ‘flawless’ to ‘hopeless.’

quotes.point: Highlights contagion and indiscriminate selling risk during stress.
quotes.text: in times of crisis, all correlations go to 1.

quotes.point: Summarizes Marks’s recommended discipline: independent valuation rather than crowd psychology.
quotes.text: Emotion? No. Analysis? Yes.
