implications.text: Treat the early-August move as evidence of sentiment-driven volatility; do not infer fundamentals from daily prices without confirming data.
Review the global book for crowded levered or carry-related exposures and for correlation assumptions that may fail in a rapid unwind.
The memo makes no Indonesia-specific claim; keep the IDR book separate and avoid importing global risk-off conclusions without local fundamental checks.
Stress-test for contagion and “all correlations go to 1” conditions, including forced-selling channels and concentration in volatile psychology-driven moves.
Use the Mr. Market framework: sell into euphoria and buy into fear only with documented independent valuation, not emotion or formula.

digests.author: Howard Marks
digests.title: The Folly of Certainty
digests.summary: Writing on July 17, 2024, Howard Marks says a New York Times article—in which Ron Klain described Jen O’Malley Dillon as having no doubt about a Biden victory—prompted a memo not on Biden’s candidacy but on how anyone can be without doubt. He cites a foreign-affairs expert’s “100% probability” that Israel would take out Iran’s nuclear capability before year-end, and the 2016 consensus that Clinton would win and that a Trump win would collapse stocks; Trump won and the market rose more than 30% over 14 months. Marks also reviews macro misses: the Fed’s “transitory” inflation view, near-certainty that rate hikes would cause recession, and rate-cut expectations that did not transpire while stocks hit new highs. He argues economies and companies can seem mechanical, but markets swing more because participant psychology and emotion are important and unpredictable; he gives 40-year standard deviations: GDP 1.8%, corporate profits 9.4%, S&P 500 price 13.1%. He recommends intellectual humility, avoiding words like “will” and “never,” and says making predictions is largely a loser’s game, reinforced by Wimbledon and the Trump assassination attempt.
key_points: Marks was prompted by a New York Times article quoting Ron Klain saying Jen O’Malley Dillon had “She doesn’t have any doubt” about Biden; he focuses on certainty, not Biden’s candidacy.
He cites a foreign-affairs expert’s “100% probability” prediction on Israel and Iran that had not come true by the memo date.
The 2016 election showed consensus error: Clinton was expected to win and a Trump win was expected to collapse stocks; Trump won and stocks rose more than 30% over 14 months.
Fed “transitory” inflation and expected recession from rate hikes are examples of macro forecasts that did not unfold as assumed; expected rate cuts also did not transpire while stocks hit highs.

Markets are harder to predict than economies or companies because psychology and emotion swamp short-run fundamentals; 40-year annual standard deviations were GDP 1.8%, corporate profits 9.4%, S&P 500 price 13.1%.
Marks recommends intellectual humility: strong beliefs while recognizing fallibility; saying “I could be wrong” prompts investigation and caution.
P.S. Wimbledon 125-to-1 winner and Trump assassination attempt reinforce that no one can state with certainty election or market impact; predictions are largely a loser’s game.

quotes.point: Marks’ core recommendation is intellectual humility in fields shaped by psychology, irrationality and randomness.
quotes.text: Doubt is not a pleasant condition, but certainty is absurd.

quotes.point: False certainty can be more dangerous than acknowledged ignorance.
quotes.text: It ain’t what you don’t know that gets you into trouble. It’s what you know for sure that just ain’t so.

quotes.point: The memo’s bottom line is skepticism toward confident macro and market forecasts.
quotes.text: making predictions is largely a loser’s game.

implications.text: Treat macro forecasts, including Fed rate-cut and election views, as scenarios with probabilities rather than certainties; check assumptions before sizing positions.
Review North book exposures that rely on a specific Fed path or election outcome; stress-test for no cuts, delayed cuts, or market reaction diverging from fundamentals.
Apply the same humility to Indonesia and IDR macro and policy forecasts; avoid assuming Fed spillovers or political outcomes will follow consensus.
Challenge language and models that imply certainty; ensure risk limits and liquidity plans do not depend on one macro forecast being right.
Remember past winners can be lucky; double-check conclusions and proceed with caution rather than extrapolating recent success.

digests.author: Howard Marks
digests.title: The Impact of Debt
digests.summary: Howard Marks's May 8, 2024 memo, prompted by Morgan Housel's April 30 article 'How I Think About Debt,' examines debt through the lens of risk and survival. Housel notes that Japan's 'shinise' — businesses operating for over 500 years — tend to hold tons of cash and no debt. Marks agrees debt is not inherently bad; the question is whether the amount is appropriate relative to the size of the enterprise and the potential for fluctuations in its profitability and asset value. Housel shows that rising indebtedness narrows the range of volatility one can withstand. Marks recalls his 2008 memo 'Volatility + Leverage = Dynamite': leverage magnifies gains and losses roughly symmetrically, but adds a risk of ruin with no corresponding upside, since a downward fluctuation can force selling or cut off credit. Because extreme volatility surfaces infrequently, calm periods tempt investors to relax rules and add leverage just before risk reappears. Attitudes toward leverage are cyclical, swinging from benign to punitive. Marks concludes the right amount is a matter of optimizing, not maximizing — err on the side of caution and margin of safety.
key_points: Studies of Japan's 'shinise' — businesses operating more than 500 years — show they tend to hold tons of cash and no debt.
Debt is not inherently bad; appropriateness depends on the size of the enterprise and the potential for fluctuations in its profitability and asset value.
Leverage amplifies gains and losses roughly symmetrically, but levered portfolios face a risk of ruin to which there is no corresponding upside.
Extreme volatility surfaces infrequently, so as calm periods pass it becomes tempting to relax rules and increase leverage, often just before risk rears its head.

Attitudes toward leverage are cyclical: in good times its favorable aspects are recognized, negative potential overlooked, lenders more willing, and regulations more permissive; the process reverses when events turn negative.
Marks cites John Mills (1865): panics do not destroy capital but reveal the extent to which it has previously been destroyed by excessive leverage in good times.
The proper amount of leverage is a matter of optimizing, not maximizing — err on the side of caution and rely on margin of safety.

quotes.point: Housel's framing, endorsed by Marks: debt reduces the set of environments a borrower can survive.
quotes.text: as debt increases, you narrow the range of outcomes you can endure in life

quotes.point: Survival requires getting through the low points, so averages are an insufficient basis for sizing leverage.
quotes.text: never forget the six-foot-tall person who drowned crossing the stream that was five feet deep on average

quotes.point: The operational rule linking asset riskiness to prudent leverage.
quotes.text: The riskier the underlying assets, the less leverage should be used to buy them.

implications.text: Stress-test leverage and financing assumptions against tail scenarios, not just 'normal levels of volatility' documented in historical statistics; include the risk that lenders cut off credit, investors withdraw equity, or covenants force selling.
Track the cyclical attitude toward leverage — permissive lending terms and relaxed rules after a good run are a signal that risk appetite, not safety, has improved.
Review gross and net leverage at position and book level and confirm each use is justified by demonstrably cautious assumptions rather than maximum availability.
Check whether leverage in Indonesia holdings or fund structures is appropriate relative to the volatility of earnings and asset values, and whether cash buffers can carry through a drawdown.

Favor optimizing over maximizing: accept good-enough returns with moderate leverage and a margin of safety rather than maximizing gains, remembering there are old investors and bold investors but not many old bold ones.

digests.author: Howard Marks (Oaktree Capital Management)
digests.title: The Indispensability of Risk
digests.summary: In this April 17, 2024 memo, Howard Marks uses a Wall Street Journal chess article by grandmaster Maurice Ashley — sent to him by his partner Bruce Karsh — as a springboard for a discussion of risk-taking. Chess distinguishes 'sham' sacrifices, where the return is immediate and calculable, from 'real' sacrifices, where gains are neither immediate nor tangible; Marks maps this onto investing, calling a 10-year U.S. Treasury note a modest or 'sham' sacrifice and most other investments real ones. He lays out three choices: avoid risk for little or no return, take modest risk for a modest return, or accept substantial uncertainty for substantial gain with the possibility of substantial permanent loss. Market efficiency, he argues, usually precludes big gains with little risk, so high returns require bearing meaningful risk — either loss in pursuit of absolute gain or underperformance in pursuit of outperformance. He warns of the risk of taking too little risk, citing backgammon, Gretzky and Kenny Smith, and his own earlier memo on Berkshire Hathaway, where success came from many decent investments, a few big winners and few big losers. The conclusion: sacrifice certainty, but do so skillfully, intelligently and with emotion under control.
key_points: Marks borrows Ashley's chess distinction between 'sham' sacrifices (calculable, immediate returns) and 'real' sacrifices (gains neither immediate nor tangible); a 10-year U.S. Treasury is offered as an investing example of the former.

Investors choose between avoiding risk for little or no return, taking modest risk for modest return, or accepting a high degree of uncertainty for substantial gain with the possibility of substantial permanent loss.
Market 'efficiency' — other participants 'aren't dummies' — usually precludes earning big gains with little risk, so high returns require bearing meaningful risk.
There is a real risk in taking too little risk: individuals may earn returns insufficient to support their cost of living, and professionals may lag client expectations or benchmarks.
Long-run high returns typically come from many well-reasoned investments, a relatively small number of big winners held heavily, and relatively few big losers — not from consistent success.
Risk-taking must be skillful: the memo closes by saying certainty must be sacrificed, but intelligently and with emotion under control.
The piece is illustrated with analogies from chess, backgammon, hockey and basketball, and quotes from Magnus Carlsen, Wayne Gretzky and Kenny Smith.

quotes.point: The memo's central thesis, quoted from Magnus Carlsen: inaction is itself a position with consequences.
quotes.text: Not being willing to take risks is an extremely risky strategy.

quotes.point: Frames under-taking risk as a return problem, relevant to benchmark and mandate compliance.
quotes.text: risk avoidance is likely to result in return avoidance

quotes.point: Guards against reading the memo as a licence for indiscriminate risk; skill and control are required.
quotes.text: You shouldn't expect to make money without bearing risk, but you shouldn't expect to make money just for taking risk.

implications.text: No market or asset view is expressed here — this is a philosophy memo, not a call. Do not read it as a signal to add risk; read it as a reminder that 'no losers' is not a usable objective and that the winner/loser ratio and the magnitude of losses relative to gains are what matter.

Consider whether Six South's current constraints are calibrated such that a well-reasoned loss is survivable. The memo explicitly warns that taking too little risk can itself fail to meet client expectations or benchmarks.

The memo's example of a 'sham' sacrifice — a 10-year U.S. Treasury, where the cost is opportunity cost and the return is contractual certainty — is a useful framing for how much of the North book is genuinely risk-bearing versus merely duration-locked.

Remember the memo's claim that market efficiency ('the other participants aren't dummies') usually precludes big gains with little risk; any macro expression pitched as high return with low risk should be treated sceptically.

When reviewing decisions, do not equate a losing position with a bad decision. Marks argues success comes from many well-reasoned investments, a small number of big winners and relatively few big losers, with some portion known in advance to fail.

digests.author: Warren E. Buffett
digests.title: Berkshire Hathaway 2023 Annual Letter
digests.summary: Warren Buffett’s 2023 Berkshire Hathaway letter opens by memorializing Charlie Munger as the architect of the present Berkshire and Buffett as the general contractor. Buffett explains Berkshire’s preferred operating earnings of $37.4 billion for 2023 versus mandated GAAP net earnings of $96 billion, arguing the latter include capricious unrealized capital gains and losses. He says Berkshire seeks enduringly good businesses run by able and trustworthy managers, but size and competition mean it has no possibility of eye-popping performance and should do only a bit better than the average American corporation with materially less risk of permanent capital loss. Berkshire holds cash and U.S. Treasury bills far above conventional needs and calls extreme fiscal conservatism a corporate pledge. It left Coke and Amex untouched, holds 27.8% of Occidental, and owns about 9% of five Japanese trading companies. BNSF and BHE disappointed; BHE faces adverse regulatory returns and forest-fire losses. Insurance performed exceptionally, setting records. Buffett says Greg Abel is ready to be CEO tomorrow.
key_points: Charlie Munger died on November 28; Buffett credits him as the architect of the present Berkshire.
Berkshire reports operating earnings of $37.4 billion for 2023 versus GAAP net earnings of $96 billion, excluding unrealized capital gains and losses.
Size and competition limit Berkshire: Buffett says there is no possibility of eye-popping performance and outside the U.S. there are essentially no meaningful candidates for capital deployment.
Berkshire emphasizes extreme fiscal conservatism, holding cash and U.S. Treasury bills far in excess of conventional wisdom.
Coke and Amex were left untouched; Berkshire owns 27.8% of Occidental and about 9% of five Japanese trading companies.
BNSF and BHE earnings disappointed; BHE faces adverse regulatory returns and forest-fire losses, while insurance set records.
Buffett says Greg Abel is in all respects ready to be CEO of Berkshire tomorrow.

quotes.point: Berkshire’s stated investment rule frames the letter’s caution.
quotes.text: Never risk permanent loss of capital.

quotes.point: Highlights valuation discipline in capital allocation.
quotes.text: All stock repurchases should be price-dependent.

quotes.point: Signals size-constrained return expectations.
quotes.text: All in all, we have no possibility of eye-popping performance.

implications.text: Use Berkshire’s stated rule as a portfolio check: never risk permanent loss of capital, and stress-test liquidity to avoid forced selling.
Assess North equity holdings on operating earnings and business quality rather than headline GAAP net income, which can swing with unrealized gains and losses.
Remember Berkshire’s own size and competition warning: expect only modest relative outperformance and do not extrapolate historical eye-popping returns.
Note the succession clarity: Buffett says Greg Abel is in all respects ready to be CEO of Berkshire tomorrow.
Do not read Berkshire’s Japanese trading-house position as an Indonesia signal; the letter says outside the U.S. there are essentially no meaningful candidates for Berkshire capital deployment.

digests.author: Howard Marks
digests.title: Easy Money
digests.summary: Howard Marks’s Jan 9 2024 memo uses Edward Chancellor’s The Price of Time to revisit his Sea Change thesis: the 2008-2021 period of declining/ultra-low rates was an “easy money” era that made business, asset appreciation, leverage, financing and avoiding default easy. Low rates reduce perceived opportunity costs, lift asset prices, encourage risk-taking and malinvestment, enable cheap and weakly documented deals, encourage leverage and liquidity mismatches, and foster expectations of continued low rates. Marks cites examples including Argentina’s 100-year bonds, low-yield LBO loans, zombie companies, Theranos, FTX and Signa. He argues cycles rhyme and credit windows open and close. Current rates are not high by history, and he doubts a return to ultra-low rates except temporarily in recessions; he guesses 2-4% base rates and a 3.0-3.5% fed funds average over 5-10 years. He warns consensus Goldilocks thinking leaves room for disappointment, while stressing Oaktree does not bet client money on macro forecasts. Different strategies may outperform versus 2009-21.
key_points: Marks revisits his Sea Change thesis: 2008-2021 was an easy-money period that made running businesses, asset appreciation, leverage, financing and avoiding default easy.
Low rates reduce perceived opportunity costs, lift asset valuations, encourage risk-taking and malinvestment, enable weak lending terms, encourage leverage and create liquidity mismatches.
Examples cited include Argentina’s 100-year bonds, low-yield LBO loans, zombie companies, Theranos, FTX and Signa.
Marks says cycles rhyme and the credit window opens and closes; excesses in one direction tend to precede corrections in the other.
He argues today’s rates are not high by historical standards and that a return to ultra-low rates is unlikely except temporarily in recessions.
His guess is 2-4% base rates and a 3.0-3.5% average fed funds rate over 5-10 years, though he stresses it is only a guess.
He warns consensus Goldilocks thinking creates room for disappointment, and says Oaktree does not bet client money on macro forecasts.

quotes.point: Munger line Marks uses to frame the behavioral risk of low rates.
quotes.text: easy money corrupts, and really easy money corrupts absolutely.

quotes.point: Credit discipline should tighten when capital is abundant.
quotes.text: the worst of loans are made at the best of times.

quotes.point: Performance in easy-money periods may reflect the environment, not skill.
quotes.text: we should never confuse brains with a bull market.

implications.text: Use Marks’s 2-4% base-rate range and 3.0-3.5% fed funds guess as scenario inputs, not forecasts; stress-test for higher-for-longer and for disappointment versus Goldilocks consensus.
Review North exposure to long-duration growth equities, long bonds, leveraged private credit/LBO loans and weak borrowers that benefited from cheap refinancing.
No Indonesia-specific claim in the memo; treat it as a global USD-rate backdrop and check South holdings for refinancing, leverage and risk-appetite sensitivity to higher USD rates.
Add checks for weak loan documentation, liquidity/liability mismatches, zombie borrowers and leverage-dependent capital structures; monitor the credit window.
Attribute past performance partly to easy money; avoid macro bets and keep bottom-up discipline, using the memo to challenge Goldilocks optimism.

digests.author: Howard Marks
digests.title: Further Thoughts on Sea Change
digests.summary: Howard Marks argues that the trends described in Sea Change are not ordinary cyclical fluctuations but a sweeping alteration of the investment environment that calls for significant capital reallocation. He recaps the 2009-21 period: the Fed held rates near zero, quantitative easing persisted, inflation stayed low, and asset owners and levered investors benefited while credit investors faced low returns. He says the roughly 2,000-basis-point decline in rates from 1980 to 2020 was probably responsible for the lion's share of investment profits, but gradual change and short financial memory made it easy to overlook. With higher inflation and faster Fed tightening, he expects tougher conditions for corporate profits, borrowing, default avoidance and asset appreciation, though he does not predict a return to 1980s rate levels or a severe recession. Credit now offers competitive contractual yields, with high yield above 8% and leveraged loans around 10%, so Marks argues for reallocation away from ownership and leverage toward lending, not dramatically increased defensiveness.
key_points: Marks says the changes in Sea Change are not just usual cyclical fluctuations; taken together, they represent a sweeping alteration of the investment environment calling for significant capital reallocation.

He argues the roughly 2,000-basis-point decline in interest rates between 1980 and 2020 was probably responsible for the lion's share of investment profits, but its gradual nature and short financial memory caused it to be overlooked.
The 2009-21 low-rate period benefited asset owners and levered investment strategies, while lending and credit investing were difficult and low-return.

Higher inflation and the Fed's faster tightening mean ultra-low or declining rates are unlikely to be the norm; possible consequences include slower growth, eroding margins, higher defaults, less reliable asset appreciation and costlier borrowing.
Credit now offers competitive contractual yields: high yield bonds yielded more than 8%, leveraged loans roughly 10%, and private loans considerably more.
Marks does not predict rates returning to 1980s highs or a severe recession or stock market collapse; he calls mainly for reallocation away from ownership and leverage toward lending.

quotes.point: Core conclusion of the sea-change thesis.
quotes.text: the easy times – and easy money – are largely over

quotes.point: Reason for recommending a significant credit allocation.
quotes.text: investors today can get equity-like returns from investments in credit

quotes.point: Warning that rate-driven gains may be mistaken for skill.
quotes.text: Never confuse brains and a bull market.

implications.text: Treat the memo as a regime-shift hypothesis, not a settled fact; Marks says the transition is early and there is no evidence yet on which to hang his hat, so track inflation and Fed policy.
Review the North book's ownership and leveraged exposures against credit opportunities; Marks argues a significant reallocation toward credit may be warranted.

Apply the credit-versus-equity framework to the South book by comparing contractual nominal yields with required returns and inflation; Marks warns nominal returns can lose value if inflation is not controlled.
Stress credit holdings for defaults and price fluctuations; Marks says isolated defaults are unlikely to derail a well-diversified portfolio, but selling in a weak period could realize losses.
Do not assume the 2009-21 playbook will persist; Marks warns against confusing brains and a bull market and says earning exceptional returns may again require bargain-purchase skill and adding value.

digests.author: Howard Marks
digests.title: Fewer Losers, or More Winners?
digests.summary: Howard Marks’s September 12, 2023 memo revisits Oaktree’s motto, “If we avoid the losers, the winners will take care of themselves,” tracing it to a 1990 dinner with General Mills pension fund head David VanBenschoten and to Benjamin Graham/Dodd’s description of fixed-income investing as a “negative art.” Marks says the motto suited high yield bond investing, where avoiding defaulters matters most, but distressed debt and “aspirational strategies” require finding or creating winners. He distinguishes risk control from risk avoidance: investing requires bearing uncertainty, and risk can be borne prudently if it is aware, analyzable, diversifiable and well paid. Using Wimbledon tennis matches, he argues outcomes depend on the balance between winners and losers, not on maximizing either alone. He discusses the “magnificent seven” stocks’ dominance of indices and the difficulty active investors face if they sell winners such as Apple. He reviews the Efficient Market Hypothesis and argues alpha—skill producing asymmetric upside/downside—can exist in practice. The memo concludes there is no universally right choice between fewer losers and more winners; it depends on skill, return aspiration and risk tolerance.
key_points: Marks traces Oaktree’s risk-control emphasis to a 1990 encounter with David VanBenschoten, whose consistent second-quartile returns ranked fourth percentile over 14 years.
The memo says avoiding losers suited high yield bond investing, but distressed debt and “aspirational strategies” require finding or creating winners.
Risk control is not risk avoidance: investing requires bearing uncertainty, and prudent risk bearing requires risk that is aware, analyzable, diversifiable and well paid.
Tennis examples show that neither maximizing winners nor minimizing losers is sufficient; the balance between winners and losers matters.
The “magnificent seven” and Apple examples show index performance can be dominated by a few stocks, and selling winners can make it hard to keep up.
Marks says alpha is skill that creates asymmetry—more upside than downside—and that the choice between fewer losers and more winners depends on skill, return aspiration and risk tolerance.

quotes.point: This is Oaktree’s motto and the memo’s core risk-control premise.
quotes.text: If we avoid the losers, the winners will take care of themselves.

quotes.point: Marks keeps risk control as Oaktree’s first tenet while distinguishing it from risk avoidance.
quotes.text: risk control isn’t everything; it is the only thing.

quotes.point: There is no universal style; the approach should match each investor’s edge and tolerance.
quotes.text: The proper choice between the two approaches – fewer losers or more winners – depends on each investor’s skill, return aspiration, and risk tolerance.

implications.text: Stress the distinction between risk control and risk avoidance; check that limits do not simply avoid uncertainty, since the memo says risk avoidance usually equates to return avoidance.

Review North and South portfolios for the balance of winners and losers rather than treating either maximizing winners or minimizing losers as sufficient; the memo says neither alone is necessarily enough.
When evaluating strategies, ask whether the manager’s claimed edge is defensive or aggressive; the memo says almost no investors possess both forms of alpha.
Remember the memo is a philosophical framework, not a current market forecast; it notes psychological excesses can change risk/return bargains but gives no timing signal.
Do not treat the memo as an Indonesia-specific signal; if applying its credit-risk comment, use it to ask whether South exposures are paid for the risk borne, not as a directive to add risk.

digests.author: Howard Marks
digests.title: Taking the Temperature
digests.summary: Howard Marks recounts five market calls he made between 2000 and 2020—the TMT bubble, the mid-2000s risk-seeking and housing excesses, the post-Lehman crisis, the 2012 'Death of Equities' parallel, and the March 2020 Covid selloff—to explain how he 'takes the temperature of the market.' He stresses that such calls are rare: his son noted he did it five times in 50 years. The memo argues that useful market judgments come less from macro forecasting or financial-statement analysis than from pattern recognition, understanding cycles as 'excesses and corrections,' and reading investor psychology when optimism or pessimism becomes extreme. At extremes, contrarianism can pay, but it requires understanding what the herd is doing and why it is wrong. Marks says Oaktree does not base decisions on macro forecasts and is not a market timer; it stays near a normal risk posture with a defensive bias, varies that posture only rarely, buys when assets are cheap rather than waiting for the bottom, and calls selling at the bottom the 'cardinal sin.'
key_points: Marks reviews five market calls: the 2000 TMT bubble, mid-2000s risk-seeking and housing excesses, post-Lehman 2008, the 2012 'Death of Equities' parallel, and March 2020 Covid.
He says his son observed he made such calls 'five times in 50 years,' emphasizing how rare high-conviction market calls are.
The memo defines cycles as a series of events each causing the next, driven by 'excesses and corrections' and investor psychology.
Taking the market's temperature relies on pattern recognition, watching for extreme optimism or pessimism, and resisting emotionality.
At extremes, Marks favors contrarianism over conformity, but says it requires understanding what the herd is doing, why, and what is wrong.
Oaktree does not base decisions on macro forecasts and is not a market timer; it normally stays near a risk posture with a defensive bias and varies only rarely.
Marks prefers buying when assets are cheap rather than waiting for the bottom, and calls selling at the bottom the 'cardinal sin' in investing.

digests.summary: Berkshire’s 2022 annual letter presents the performance table for 1965–2022, showing compounded annual gain of 19.8% versus 9.9% for the S&P 500 with dividends, and overall gain of 3,787,464% versus 24,708%. Buffett reports 2022 operating earnings of a record $30.8 billion and argues quarterly GAAP earnings are misleading because capital gains and losses swing wildly. He describes the Alleghany purchase and insurance float rising from $147 billion to $164 billion, with disciplined underwriting giving a decent chance of cost-free float over time. Berkshire repurchased 1.2% of its shares, and Buffett defends value-accretive repurchases while warning that overpaying hurts continuing shareholders. He says Berkshire will always hold a boatload of cash and U.S. Treasury bills and avoid behavior that could create uncomfortable cash needs; the CEO will always be Chief Risk Officer. He calls near-term economic and market forecasts worse than useless, cites huge fiscal deficits, says Berkshire offers only modest, imperfect inflation protection, and reiterates long-term faith in America and the value of a great partner.

digests.author: Howard Marks
digests.title: 2020 in Review
digests.summary: Howard Marks reviews 2020 as a year of extremes: the worst pandemic in over a century, the worst quarterly U.S. real GDP drop in recorded quarterly history, then the biggest annualized gain; a sharp S&P 500 fall and rapid recovery; record fiscal and monetary support; and record high yield and investment grade issuance. He argues aggressive Fed and Treasury actions explain the anomalous combination of health emergency, weak economy and strong capital and stock markets. The buying opportunity was brief, panic was limited, and defaults came nowhere near predictions. For 2021, Marks sees positives: a likely healthy economy, accommodative Fed, reopening and vaccine rollout, stimulus, pent-up demand, extra disposable income and reduced political uncertainty. Risks include rising interest rates as the biggest risk, inflation uncertainty, vaccine disappointment, speculative market behavior, high valuations, narrow risk compensation, Washington policy, China tensions, social divisions, dollar/reserve-currency questions and automation. He calls valuations a gray area—not low, mostly high side of fair, not unreasonable—and does not make a compelling top call. He favors a normal stance with a modest defensive bias and preparation for inflation and higher rates.

digests.author: Terry Smith
digests.title: Fundsmith Equity Fund Letter to Shareholders
digests.summary: Terry Smith’s letter dated 31 March 2020 updates investors on Fundsmith Equity Fund during the Covid-19 pandemic. He says the Fund continues to operate: it can be priced, investors can deal, and liquidity has been provided where required. Year to date the Fund was down 7.9%, versus MSCI World -15.7%, MSCI World Value -22.0% and FTSE 100 -23.8%. Smith says performance was as expected and satisfactory given some valuation fall is inevitable in a bear market. He restates scepticism that so-called value stocks protect in downturns, arguing lowly rated companies are often cyclical, leveraged, low-return or structurally challenged. Amadeus and InterContinental Hotels are taking cost-cutting, cash-conservation and liquidity measures to withstand about 18 months with no revenues; if their equity were vaporised the Fund would lose about 5% of the portfolio. He estimates about a third of the portfolio may see increased revenues this year, citing Microsoft, payment processors, Clorox and Reckitt Benckiser. The Fund bought two new holdings hit by China exposure and a classic “glitch”. Smith compares the economy’s weakened state to a vulnerable immune system and says he focuses on what he can affect.

digests.author: Warren E. Buffett
digests.title: Berkshire Hathaway Inc. — 2019 Annual Letter
digests.summary: Berkshire’s 2019 GAAP earnings were $81.4 billion, including $24 billion of operating earnings, $3.7 billion of realized capital gains and a $53.7 billion increase in net unrealized gains. Buffett and Munger disagree with the 2018 GAAP rule that puts unrealized equity swings into earnings and urge shareholders to focus on operating earnings. The letter emphasizes retained earnings: Berkshire’s ten largest stock holdings paid $3.798 billion in dividends while Berkshire’s share of their retained earnings was $8.332 billion. Controlled non-insurance businesses earned $17.7 billion, up 3%, with BNSF and BHE contributing $8.3 billion, up 6%. P/C float reached $129.423 billion; Berkshire had an underwriting profit in 16 of the last 17 years, but Buffett warns that mega-catastrophe or cyber losses will come. BHE has retained $28 billion and expects Iowa wind self-sufficiency in 2021. Equity holdings were carried at $248 billion market versus $110.34 billion cost; Buffett says they earn more than 20% on net tangible equity without excessive debt and, if rates and taxes stay low, equities should beat long-term fixed debt—though major drops are possible. He says Berkshire is prepared for succession, and his will directs Berkshire shares to be held and distributed over an estimated 12 to 15 years. The letter also critiques board independence and discusses $5 billion of 2019 buybacks.

digests.author: Terry Smith (CEO, Fundsmith LLP)
digests.title: Fundsmith Equity Fund — First Annual Letter to Owners
digests.summary: Terry Smith's first annual letter to owners of The Fundsmith Equity Fund covers the period from the fund's 1 November 2010 launch to 31 December 2010. The fund rose 6.14% net of fees, versus MSCI 7.99%, MSCI EAFE 5.76%, FTSE100 4.40% and a 10-year UK Treasury long bond at -2.57%. Smith says benchmarks are useful over long periods but should not drive portfolio construction. Del Monte Foods was the main positive contributor; the letter uses pet food to illustrate the small-ticket, non-durable, brand-loyal, replenishment characteristics he seeks. Other contributors were Becton Dickinson, Domino's Pizza Inc, Nestle and Stryker; detractors were Serco Group, Imperial Tobacco, Dr Pepper Snapple and Reckitt Benckiser. At year-end the fund held 22 stocks with an average founding year of 1883, a trailing free cash flow yield of about 7%, average return on operating assets of 50%, and a 2.47% dividend yield covered over 2.5 times. Smith warns about synthetic ETF counterparty risk and leveraged/inverse ETF daily compounding. He is cautious on a sustained major-economy recovery and on equities generally as cheap, while constructive on the fund's portfolio.

digests.author: Alan I. Kirshner; Anthony F. Markel; Steven A. Markel; Darrell D. Martin
digests.title: Markel Corporation 2002 Annual Letter
digests.summary: Markel Corporation's 2002 annual letter reviews a year in which the company focused its international business under the Markel brand, reduced gross premiums during restructuring, and saw underwriting discipline and improved pricing return to its markets. It absorbed $69 million of underwriting losses from discontinued lines, mainly due to higher asbestos reserves, and increased reserves mostly in North America after claims worsened. Corifrance remained in discontinued operations but was not discontinued. Investments returned 8.3% overall: fixed income 9.8%, equities -8.8%, better than the S&P 500 but disappointing. Equities were 13% of the portfolio and 48% of shareholders' equity, below preferred levels; Markel was increasing allocation where it saw quality at favorable prices while remaining cautious on bond duration given low rates. Investments and cash rose 20% to $4.3 billion, investment leverage increased, and shareholders' equity reached $1.2 billion. Management discusses reserve adequacy, unearned premium, a February 2003 $200 million note issuance, corporate governance and owner-partnership principles, and a constructive view of insurance pricing and long-term investing.

Investments and cash rose 20% to $4.3 billion; investment leverage was 3.7 times shareholders' equity versus 3.3 times a year earlier.
Shareholders' equity reached $1.2 billion, or $118 per share, with 6.7% growth.

digests.author: Markel Corporation (signed by Alan I. Kirshner, Anthony F. Markel, Steven A. Markel, Darrell D. Martin, Paul W. Springman, Thomas S. Gayner)
digests.title: Markel Corporation 2004 Annual Letter to Business Partners
digests.summary: Markel's 2004 annual letter marks the company's forthcoming 75th anniversary and reviews a record year. It reports earned premiums above $2 billion, a 96% combined ratio, net income of $165 million, comprehensive income of $273 million, and shareholders' equity of $1.7 billion, or $168.22 per share. Book value per share compounded at 24% annually since the 1986 IPO, with 20% compound growth over the prior one- and five-year periods and 21% over ten years. Results absorbed about $80 million of Florida hurricane losses; management calls the business lumpy and says it expects the unexpected. Insurance pricing stabilized after 2001-2003 increases and was showing weakness, with gross written premiums down 2% while net written premiums rose 4% and earned premiums rose 10%. Markel says it will not chase business without adequate pricing and puts underwriting profits first. Investments returned 7.9% taxable equivalent, with equities at 15.2% and fixed maturities at 4.8%; equities rose to $1.3 billion, 21% of the portfolio and 81% of equity. Fixed income remains short duration and high quality on concern rates may rise. London produced about 28% of gross premium but no underwriting profit yet. Darrell Martin will hand CFO duties to Richie Whitt.

digests.author: Terry Smith, CEO, Fundsmith LLP
digests.title: Fundsmith Equity Fund annual letter to shareholders 2012
digests.summary: Terry Smith’s January 2013 letter reports that the Fundsmith Equity Fund rose 12.5% in 2012, versus 11.4% for the MSCI World Index in sterling, and returned 12.6% annualised since inception versus 6.6%. He cautions that calendar-year periods are too short and says Fundsmith seeks long-term outperformance rather than beating the market in every period or condition. He is surprised the fund outperformed in a year when central-bank liquidity buoyed risk assets, including banks, Greek bonds and other assets the fund would not own; he says it will never own bank stocks. Portfolio turnover was 0.48%, the fund ended with 28 holdings, and the OCF is expected to be 16bps. The weighted average free cash flow yield was about 5.7%, return on capital averaged about 32%, and historical dividend yield was 2.3%. Smith warns that record-low rates have driven a desperate search for yield into junk bonds, emerging-market debt, CLOs and high-yielding equities, and criticises income funds that charge expenses to capital. He expects more QE and central-bank mandate changes, warning of inflation and currency depreciation, but says macro views do not affect strategy.

digests.author: Terry Smith, CEO, Fundsmith LLP
digests.title: Fundsmith Equity Fund Annual Letter to Shareholders 2013
digests.summary: The Fundsmith Equity Fund’s fourth annual letter reports a 25.3% total return for 2013 versus 24.3% for the MSCI World Index in sterling, and 62.2% cumulative and 16.5% annualised since inception on 1 November 2010. Terry Smith says the portfolio could be called “defensive” yet outperformed a bullish market by 1%. He describes 2013 as roughly two halves, with the market falling after Bernanke’s May tapering comments and recovering as authorities backed down. He is sceptical about the strength of economic recovery because underlying revenue growth across the 64-stock Investable Universe slowed by a couple of percentage points, while consumer markets are not improving significantly. The fund remained fully invested in high-quality companies, sold five holdings, bought C.R. Bard and began buying an undisclosed transaction-services company. Turnover was low and dealing costs were 2.5bps. Portfolio FCF yield fell from 5.7% to 5.1%; ROCE averaged 34% and cash conversion typically 90-100%. Smith warns valuation gains have been driven by QE and ZIRP and may be temporary, and announces a 2014 Emerging Equities Trust.

He criticises performance measurement over short periods. The letter says the approach is not based on a global economic outlook or market-timing judgments; the Fund aims to be fully invested in good companies that create value. digests.author: Markel Corporation executive team
digests.title: Markel Corporation 2005 Annual Letter to Business Partners
digests.summary: Markel’s 2005 letter reports that most businesses performed well, but hurricane losses drove results below expectations. Underwriting excluding hurricanes produced $234 million of profit, yet Katrina, Rita and Wilma losses of $246 million left a $12 million underwriting loss. Net income was $148 million and comprehensive earnings $64 million; the combined ratio rose to 101% from 96%, with hurricanes adding about 12 points. Operating revenues fell 3% to $2.2 billion as competition increased and gross written premiums declined 5%. Investment income rose 19% to $242 million, but total portfolio return was about 1.5% after foreign exchange losses, reflecting rising rates and a sideways equity market. Markel says catastrophes are normal, expects future losses, and aims to earn enough in good years to offset bad ones while managing aggregate exposures. It is raising prices, reducing limits, increasing deductibles and relying less on industry catastrophe models. The letter also describes disciplined walking away from underpriced business, cautious fixed-income duration, a long-term equity approach, private investments, improved reserve development and a $200 million buyback authorization. Management calls 2005 short of expectations but remains optimistic about 2006 and long-term prospects.

quotes.point: Explains Markel’s short-duration, high-credit-quality fixed income stance.

digests.author: Markel Corporation executive team (Thomas S. Gayner and fellow signatories)
digests.title: Markel Corporation 2006 Annual Letter to Business Partners
digests.summary: Markel’s 2006 letter reports record underwriting profit, superior investment returns and strong book-value growth in its 20th year as a public company. Gross written premiums rose 6% to $2.5 billion and earned premiums 13% to $2.2 billion; the combined ratio improved to 87% from 101%, and net income reached a record $393 million versus $148 million. Book value per share increased 32% to about $230. Management credits associates but also says results included “a large dose of good luck” from extremely benign weather, and notes 2005 hurricane losses of $301 million. The investment portfolio grew 14% to $7.5 billion; net investment income rose 12% to $271 million, realized gains were $64 million, and taxable-equivalent total return was 11.2%. The letter emphasizes long-term horizon, discipline and continuous learning across underwriting and investing. It warns that seeking premium growth at the expense of underwriting profits “always leads to disaster,” cautions that crowded private equity and hedge funds may disappoint due to fees and short-term management, and describes a conservative loss-reserve philosophy with a margin of safety.
key_points: 2006 results: gross written premiums +6% to $2.5 billion, earned premiums +13% to $2.2 billion, combined ratio 87% vs 101%, net income $393 million vs $148 million, book value per share +32% to about $230.
Management says 2006 included “a large dose of good luck” from benign weather; catastrophe-exposure improvements were not tested, and 2005 hurricanes produced $301 million of underwriting losses.
Investment portfolio grew 14% to $7.5 billion; net investment income rose 12% to $271 million, realized gains were $64 million, and taxable-equivalent total return was 11.2%.
The letter stresses long-term horizon, discipline and continuous learning, warning that premium growth at the expense of underwriting profits “always leads to disaster.”

Private equity and hedge funds are described as “white hot”; Markel expects many investors to be disappointed by high fees and short-term management, and prefers measured direct private-equity investing.
Loss reserves are set with a margin of safety; unpaid losses were $4.3 billion, about 60% IBNR, and management says insurance surprises are almost always bad.

Balance sheet strength: operating cash flow $512 million, debt to total capital 27%, $150 million of 7.50% senior notes issued, about 140,000 shares repurchased at $328, and Lemuel E. Lewis added to the board.

quotes.point: Management attributes part of the strong result to benign catastrophe weather, so the combined ratio should not be treated as a clean run-rate.
quotes.text: our 2006 results include a large dose of good luck as the weather was extremely benign.

quotes.point: Underwriting discipline is central; premium growth without profit is framed as a path to disaster.
quotes.text: A great and common danger in the insurance business is to seek premium growth at the expense of underwriting profits.

quotes.point: Supports long holding periods and tax-deferred compounding rather than trading on macro forecasts.
quotes.text: Our ideal investment is one that we can own forever.

implications.text: Do not extrapolate Markel’s 87% combined ratio as a clean run-rate: management explicitly attributes part of 2006 to benign weather and says catastrophe changes were not tested. Stress catastrophe assumptions.
When reviewing insurance or financial holdings, test underwriting discipline and reserve conservatism, not just reported combined ratios; the letter flags reserve surprises as almost always bad.
Keep process disciplined through underperformance and avoid style drift; Markel warns investors often abandon sound discipline after short-term underperformance and crowd into what others are doing.
Avoid relying on forecasts of rates, oil, FX, geopolitics or hurricane frequency; management argues such forecasting cannot be done reliably and favors business fundamentals and valuation.

Assess management on honesty and talent, capital allocation, reinvestment opportunities and fair price—the letter’s four-part equity philosophy—and note its skepticism toward stock options versus share ownership.

Gross written premiums fell 7% to $2.4 billion, but Markel reported $264 million of underwriting profit and an 88% combined ratio.

Net investment income rose 13% to $306 million; the investment portfolio was $7.8 billion and shareholders' equity $2.6 billion, with investment leverage down from just under 4:1 to just under 3:1.
Total investment return was 4.8%: fixed income returned 5.6% and equities lost 0.4%; Markel credits its high-quality, minimal-credit-risk fixed income approach.

Markel Re's SMART line had underwriting losses from delegated underwriting authority without sufficient oversight; three profitable Markel Re products will move to Markel Underwriting Managers in 1Q08.

Markel International reported $46 million of underwriting profit and a 93% combined ratio; executive bonuses are tied to five-year book-value-per-share growth, and associates owned over 10% of shares.

quotes.point: Signals underwriting discipline amid a softer, more competitive insurance market.
quotes.text: For Markel, this environment calls for caution.

quotes.point: Frames pricing pressure as a capital-driven insurance-cycle issue.
quotes.text: the industry has too much capital and, therefore, increased competition.

quotes.point: Shows a constructive long-term view of financial-system normalcy despite near-term stress.
quotes.text: The current financial crunch will heal and pass as all others have done before.

implications.text: Markel describes excess P&C capital and soft pricing as worldwide dynamics; monitor insurance-cycle pricing and underwriting-margin pressure rather than premium growth alone.

Use Markel's plain-vanilla, high-quality fixed income stance and four-part equity philosophy as a checklist; note its 2007 equity drag from financials and consumer holdings and minimal energy/commodity exposure.
Remember Markel says the same competitive insurance dynamics are occurring in the worldwide market; check whether any South insurance-linked exposures face similar capital and pricing pressure.
The SMART losses came from delegated underwriting authority without sufficient oversight; review third-party underwriting/agent oversight and reserve conservatism in insurance-linked exposures.
Judge insurance holdings on combined ratio, underwriting profit and five-year book-value compounding; do not reward premium growth without profitable underwriting.

digests.author: Warren Buffett
digests.title: Berkshire Hathaway Inc. 2004 Annual Letter to Shareholders
digests.summary: Berkshire's 2004 net-worth gain was $8.3 billion, raising per-share book value 10.5%, slightly below the S&P 500's 10.9% return. Over 40 years, book value grew from $19 to $55,824, a 21.9% compounded rate, though Buffett says per-share intrinsic value matters more than book. Equity holdings have fallen below 50% of net worth, so yearly market moves affect a smaller portion of Berkshire than before. The letter reports $43 billion of cash equivalents after Buffett struck out on multi-billion acquisitions and found few attractive securities, a position he calls not happy. Insurance float reached $46.1 billion with $1.551 billion of underwriting profit; NICO's disciplined underwriting and GEICO's low-cost model are praised. Buffett warns investors that high costs, tips and fads, and start-stop timing hurt returns, and that last year's near-average market return was unusual. Reinsurance discusses a possible $100 billion catastrophe, with Berkshire prepared for a 3%-5% loss share. Manufacturing, service and retailing earned 21.7% on average tangible net worth. Common stocks are viewed as fractional ownership in businesses, not trading vehicles.
key_points: 2004 net worth rose $8.3 billion and per-share book value rose 10.5%, versus a 10.9% S&P 500 return; 1965-2004 book value compounded at 21.9%.
The letter says intrinsic value matters more than book value, and equity holdings have fallen to less than 50% of net worth from an average of 114% in the 1980s.
Berkshire ended 2004 with $43 billion of cash equivalents after no multi-billion acquisitions and few attractive securities; Buffett calls this 'not a happy position.'
Insurance float reached $46.1 billion and underwriting profit was $1.551 billion; NICO's disciplined underwriting and GEICO's low-cost model are highlighted.
Investors are warned that high costs, tips and fads, and start-stop market timing cause poor outcomes; excitement and expenses are called enemies.
Reinsurance commentary says a $100 billion catastrophe is possible and Berkshire is prepared for a 3%-5% loss share; 2005 pricing is expected to be less attractive.
Manufacturing, service and retailing operations earned 21.7% on average tangible net worth, and common stocks are treated as fractional ownership in businesses.

quotes.point: Shows cash was high because attractive acquisitions and securities were scarce, not because Buffett was pleased with idle cash.
quotes.text: Berkshire therefore ended the year with $43 billion of cash equivalents, not a happy position.

quotes.point: Frames cost control and emotional discipline as controllable drags on investor returns.
quotes.text: Investors should remember that excitement and expenses are their enemies.

quotes.point: Supports cautious due diligence on leveraged, financial and derivative exposures whose marks can be fuzzy.
quotes.text: You only learn who has been swimming naked when the tide goes out.

implications.text: Use the letter's view that future S&P returns are expected below the 35-year 11.2% average to avoid extrapolating recent U.S. equity returns into Six South forecasts.
Check whether North's cash weight is a deliberate valuation discipline or an absence of attractive ideas; the letter treats high cash as unhappy but does not endorse forcing purchases.
Do not infer an Indonesia or IDR signal from this U.S.-centric letter; keep South's positioning driven by its own local evidence.
Stress-test tail events and liquidity, remembering the letter's warning that a $100 billion catastrophe is possible and derivative marks can be fuzzy.
Review turnover, fees and start-stop entry and exit behavior against Buffett's warning that excitement and expenses are investors' enemies.

digests.author: Warren Buffett
digests.title: Berkshire Hathaway Inc. 2005 Chairman's Letter
digests.summary: Berkshire’s 2005 net worth gain was $5.6 billion, raising per-share book value by 6.4%; over 41 years book value compounded at 21.5%, from $19 to $59,377. Buffett calls 2005 decent: five acquisitions were initiated (two not yet closed) and most operating subsidiaries prospered, while insurance as a whole did well despite Hurricane Katrina losses estimated at $2.5 billion and $0.9 billion more from Rita and Wilma. GEICO improved productivity 32% in two years, cut employment 4% while policies grew 26%, and raised auto policies in force 12.1%, lifting U.S. private passenger market share from about 5.6% to 6.1%. Float reached $49 billion and was costless in 2005 despite $3.4 billion of hurricane losses. Because hurricane frequency/intensity is uncertain, Berkshire will write mega-cat only at much higher prices and limited aggregate exposure. Acquisitions included MedPro, Forest River, Business Wire, Applied Underwriters and PacifiCorp. Gen Re derivative exit lost $104 million pre-tax in 2005, $404 million cumulatively; Buffett warns derivative contracts continue to mushroom. He expects no miracles from the equity portfolio, sees 6-8% per-share earnings growth and roughly matching stock prices over a decade, and criticizes fixed-price options.
key_points: 2005 net worth gain was $5.6 billion and per-share book value rose 6.4%; 1965-2005 book value compounded at 21.5% to $59,377.
Five acquisitions were initiated, two not yet closed, including MedPro, Forest River, Business Wire, Applied Underwriters and PacifiCorp; none involved issuing Berkshire shares.
Insurance float reached $49 billion and was costless in 2005 despite $3.4 billion of hurricane losses; Katrina cost an estimated $2.5 billion, with $0.9 billion more from Rita and Wilma.
GEICO improved productivity 32% in two years, cut employment 4% while policies grew 26%, and increased auto policies in force 12.1%, lifting market share from about 5.6% to 6.1%.
Due to uncertain hurricane frequency/intensity, Berkshire will write mega-cat policies only at far higher prices and with aggregate exposure that would not cause distress.
Gen Re’s derivative exit lost $104 million pre-tax in 2005 and $404 million cumulatively; Buffett warns derivative contracts outstanding worldwide continue to mushroom.
The equity portfolio is not bargain-priced; Buffett expects 6-8% per-share earnings growth and stock prices roughly matching over a decade, and criticizes fixed-price options.

quotes.point: Sets the year’s headline result and per-share book-value gain.
quotes.text: Our gain in net worth during 2005 was $5.6 billion

quotes.point: Signals tighter catastrophe underwriting and tail-risk caution.
quotes.text: we should now write mega-cat policies only at prices far higher than prevailed last year

quotes.point: Temper return expectations for high-quality equity holdings.
quotes.text: Expect no miracles from our equity portfolio.

implications.text: Track hurricane/climate uncertainty and derivative-market growth as tail risks; the letter says recent storm experience is worrisome and derivative contracts outstanding continue to mushroom.

Do not treat Berkshire’s equity holdings as bargains: management expects 6-8% per-share earnings growth and stock prices to roughly match over a decade; revisit North valuation assumptions for quality compounders.
No Indonesia-specific signal appears in the document; keep South theses independent rather than importing U.S. insurance/utility read-across.

Review long-dated or illiquid derivative and mark-to-market exposures for valuation asymmetry and liquidity mismatch; Buffett warns two parties can report paper profits and valuation differences tend to favor higher earnings.
Scrutinize management compensation and capital allocation: fixed-price options can reward retained earnings and repurchases even when the business does not improve.

digests.author: Warren Buffett
digests.title: Berkshire Hathaway Inc. 2006 Annual Letter to Shareholders
digests.summary: Berkshire's 2006 letter reports a $16.9 billion gain in net worth and an 18.4% increase in per-share book value, with 21.4% compounded annual growth since 1965. Buffett credits insurance with a large dose of luck because major hurricanes did not hit, and highlights GEICO's growth: policies rose from 5.7 million to 8.1 million between 2003 and 2006 while full-time-equivalent employees fell 3.5%, a 47% productivity gain. Acquisitions included 80% of ISCAR for $4 billion, TTI and Fruit tuck-ins. Float reached $50.9 billion, and the Equitas retroactive reinsurance contract adds about $7 billion. Buffett warns that super-cat rates have fallen with incoming capital, so Berkshire sharply reduced wind exposures, and says Katrina is not close to a worst-case event. The letter flags weakening residential housing and mortgage practices, eroding newspaper economics, and U.S. trade deficits that turned the investment income account negative in 2006. It also discusses retroactive reinsurance accounting, MidAmerican, NetJets, Clayton, common-stock holdings and a nearly eliminated direct foreign-exchange position.
key_points: 2006 net worth gain was $16.9 billion; per-share book value rose 18.4%, and compounded annual growth from 1965 through 2006 was 21.4%.
Insurance benefited from an absence of major hurricanes; float reached $50.9 billion, and the Equitas retroactive reinsurance contract adds about $7 billion.
Super-cat rates fell as capital entered the field, so Berkshire sharply reduced wind exposures; Buffett says it is naive to treat Katrina as close to a worst-case event.
GEICO policies rose from 5.7 million to 8.1 million between yearend 2003 and 2006 while full-time-equivalent employees fell 3.5%, a 47% productivity gain.
The manufacturing, service and retailing group earned 25% on average tangible net worth but 10.8% on average carrying value because of purchase premiums.
HomeServices volume fell 9% and profits fell 50%; Buffett links the housing slowdown partly to weakened lending practices, optional contracts and teaser rates.
Newspaper economics are eroding, and Buffett expects Buffalo News profit margins to slide; the direct foreign-exchange position is nearly eliminated after a $2.2 billion gain since 2002.

quotes.point: This is the letter's explicit price-discipline rule for markets and risk-taking.
quotes.text: Be fearful when others are greedy, and be greedy when others are fearful.

quotes.point: It explains why Berkshire cut wind exposures when super-cat rates fell.
quotes.text: Appropriate prices don’t guarantee profits in any given year, but inappropriate prices most certainly guarantee eventual losses.

quotes.point: It signals that super-cat loss estimates should not be anchored to a single historical event.
quotes.text: It’s naïve to think of Katrina as anything close to a worst-case event.

implications.text: Monitor the U.S. trade deficit and dollar risk: the letter says the investment income account turned negative in 2006 and expects dollar weakness over time; it calls a soft landing wishful thinking.
Keep valuation and price discipline: use the 'fearful when greedy' rule and avoid exposures at prices that do not reflect loss probabilities, especially where capital inflows have compressed rates.
No Indonesia-specific claim appears in the document; treat the U.S. housing, dollar and super-cat warnings as global context, not direct IDR-book signals, unless local evidence confirms.

Review super-cat/wind and retroactive reinsurance exposures: Berkshire cut wind exposures after rates fell, and Equitas raises the annual DCRA charge to about $450 million, a hurdle for cost-free float.

Evaluate businesses on multiple yardsticks and industry economics: the letter highlights per-share investments and pre-tax non-insurance earnings, and warns that eroding fundamentals can overwhelm talented management.

digests.author: Terry Smith
digests.title: Annual Letter to Shareholders 2015
digests.summary: Terry Smith’s sixth annual letter to Fundsmith Equity Fund owners reports a +15.7% total return for 2015 versus +4.9% for the MSCI World Index in sterling, a 10.8% outperformance and the fifth consecutive year of outperformance. Since inception on 1 November 2010, the Fund returned +131.4% cumulative and +17.6% annualised, against +64.3% and +10.1% for the index. The letter notes negative or weak returns for the FTSE 100 and S&P 500 in 2015 and discusses warnings that highly rated ‘bond proxies’ may suffer as US rates rise. Smith doubts the simplicity of the claim, notes the Fed only sets short-term rates, and questions suggested switches into cyclicals. Look-through portfolio metrics show higher ROCE, gross and operating margins, cash conversion and interest cover, and lower leverage than the FTSE 100 and S&P 500. The portfolio’s weighted average FCF yield was 4.3% at year-end versus 4.5% at the start, while FCF per share grew 9.7%. Portfolio turnover was 2%, and TCI was 1.13% versus OCF 1.07%. The letter lists top and bottom contributors, sales of Domino’s Pizza, Choice Hotels and eBay, retention of PayPal, a new Waters Corporation holding, and concern about Procter & Gamble’s third internally sourced CEO in as many years.
key_points: Fund returned +15.7% in 2015 versus +4.9% for the MSCI World Index in sterling, its fifth consecutive year of outperformance; cumulative return since inception was +131.4%.
The letter challenges the ‘bond proxies’ warning, noting the Fed sets short-term rates while longer-term US rates are set by Treasury and swap markets.
Look-through quality metrics were ROCE 26.0%, gross margin 61.1%, cash conversion 98.4%, leverage 29.3% and interest cover 16.1x versus FTSE 100 and S&P 500 averages.
Weighted average FCF yield was 4.3% at year-end versus 4.5% at the start; FCF per share grew 9.7% on average.
Portfolio turnover was 2%; voluntary dealing cost £496,507 or 1.4 basis points; TCI was 1.13% versus OCF of 1.07%.
Sold Domino’s Pizza, Choice Hotels and eBay; retained PayPal; built a holding in Waters Corporation; flagged Procter & Gamble’s third internally sourced CEO in as many years.

quotes.point: Establishes the track record central to the letter.
quotes.text: The Fund therefore outperformed the market in 2015 by 10.8%, its fifth consecutive year of outperformance

quotes.point: States the core investment strategy.
quotes.text: we seek to own shares in good companies and at least most of the time we succeed in that objective.

quotes.point: Highlights fundamental growth versus valuation change.
quotes.text: Our companies on average grew their free cash flow per share by 9.7%* during the year

implications.text: Use Fundsmith’s look-through quality checklist—ROCE, margins, cash conversion, leverage and interest cover—when reviewing global holdings; the letter reports portfolio metrics above FTSE 100 and S&P 500 averages.
Do not treat a Fed short-rate move as automatically setting long-term rates; the letter notes long-term US rates are set by Treasury and swap markets.
Check rate-sensitivity and ‘bond proxy’ assumptions rather than assuming rotation into cyclicals is the answer; Fundsmith questions that trade.
Remember the letter’s preference for low turnover and cost control: portfolio turnover was 2%, and TCI (1.13%) included dealing costs beyond the OCF (1.07%).
Flag Procter & Gamble’s third internally sourced CEO in as many years as a succession/governance concern noted by Fundsmith.

digests.author: Terry Smith
digests.title: Fundsmith Equity Fund 2016 Annual Letter to Shareholders
digests.summary: Terry Smith's January 2017 annual letter reports Fundsmith Equity Fund returned +28.2% in 2016, matching the MSCI World Index in sterling, and +196.6% cumulative since inception versus +110.6% for that benchmark; annualised returns were +19.3% versus +12.8%. The Fund beat the FTSE 100's +19.2% total return by +9%. First-half performance (+16.4% versus +11.0%) was aided by the pound's fall after the Brexit vote; in the second half a rotation toward banks and cyclicals, linked to expectations for faster US growth after Trump's election, saw its sectors underperform. Smith defends the quality strategy against warnings on consumer staples and 'bond proxies', dismisses macro forecasting as a second-order system, and notes the Fed raised rates by only 0.5% over a year. Look-through portfolio metrics show ROCE of 26.7%, gross margin 61.9%, cash conversion 99.4%, leverage 37.7% and interest cover 17.0x, versus lower/weaker index averages. Free cash flow grew just over 11%; the FCF yield ended at 4.4%. Turnover was -15.6%, and TCI was 1.11% versus OCF 1.06%. He cites Domino's 45% rise after sale as a caution.
key_points: Fund returned +28.2% in 2016, matching MSCI World in sterling; cumulative +196.6% since inception vs +110.6%, annualised +19.3% vs +12.8%.
First half +16.4% vs +11.0% aided by pound fall post-Brexit; second half rotation toward banks/cyclicals linked to Trump growth expectations hurt relative performance.
Smith rejects macro prediction as a basis for investment, calling markets a second-order system; lists Brexit, China, India demonetisation, elections, rates and Trump as uncontrollable factors.
Look-through quality metrics: ROCE 26.7%, gross margin 61.9%, operating margin 25.5%, cash conversion 99.4%, leverage 37.7%, interest cover 17.0x vs indices.
FCF grew just over 11%; FCF yield was 4.3% at start and 4.4% at end, so the portfolio did not become more highly rated.
Turnover was -15.6%; TCI was 1.11% vs OCF 1.06%; voluntary dealing was £181,025 or 0.003% of the Fund.
P&G was sold in January 2016; Domino's, sold in 2015, rose +45% in 2016, illustrating reluctance to sell good companies.

quotes.point: Supports Smith's argument that macro predictions are insufficient unless an investor also gauges market expectations.
quotes.text: Markets are a so-called second-order system

quotes.point: Frames the quality screen behind the portfolio's superior look-through ROCE and margins.
quotes.text: Consistently high returns on capital are one sign we look for when seeking companies to invest in.

quotes.point: Highlights why total cost including dealing, or TCI, matters when assessing fund costs.
quotes.text: The OCF does not include an important element of costs - the costs of dealing.

implications.text: Do not turn the letter's macro list into forecasts: Smith argues even correct predictions must be weighed against what markets expect, so use it as risk awareness only.
When reviewing global holdings, compare look-through ROCE, margins, cash conversion, leverage, interest cover and FCF yield versus indices; the letter shows quality and valuation can coexist.
Remember the letter provides no Indonesia-specific analysis; its only South Asia macro reference is 'Demonetisation' in India, so do not extrapolate it to the IDR book without separate work.

Flag narrative risk around consumer staples and 'bond proxies': the letter says those stocks underperformed in 2016 despite being cited as popular, so monitor label-versus-performance and sector rotation.
When evaluating managers, ask for TCI including dealing costs and turnover alongside OCF, and weigh process consistency against short-term sector rotation.

digests.author: Terry Smith, CEO, Fundsmith LLP
digests.title: Annual Letter to Shareholders 2017
digests.summary: Terry Smith’s eighth annual letter reports that the Fundsmith Equity Fund’s T Class Accumulation shares returned +22.0% in 2017, versus +11.8% for the MSCI World Index in sterling and +12.0% for the FTSE 100. Since inception on 1 November 2010 the Fund returned +261.7% cumulative and +19.7% annualised. Smith says 2017 featured a sector rotation away from the Fund’s holdings toward banks and cyclicals, linked to expectations of stronger growth and US policy after Donald Trump’s election. He dismisses macro forecasting, compares post-crisis conditions to the Long Depression of 1873–96, and argues debt is higher than in 2007 and low rates may persist. The portfolio’s companies show higher ROCE, margins, cash conversion and lower leverage than the S&P 500 and FTSE 100; weighted free cash flow grew 13%. The portfolio FCF yield fell from 4.4% to 3.7%, partly because Imperial Brands and J M Smucker were sold and Intuit bought. Turnover was 5.4% and TCI 1.08%. The letter also discusses activism and takeovers at ADP, Nestlé, P&G and Unilever/Kraft Heinz.
key_points: Fundsmith Equity Fund T Class Accumulation returned +22.0% in 2017 versus +11.8% for MSCI World in sterling and +12.0% for FTSE 100; cumulative return since inception was +261.7%, annualised +19.7%.
Smith describes 2017 as a sector rotation away from the Fund’s holdings toward banks and cyclicals, tied to expectations of stronger growth and US policy after Donald Trump’s election.
He is sceptical of macro predictions, invokes the Long Depression of 1873–96, says there is more debt now than in 2007, and suggests low rates and sluggish growth may persist.
Portfolio companies had 28% ROCE, 63% gross margin, 26% operating margin, 102% cash conversion and 37% leverage versus S&P 500 and FTSE 100 averages; weighted free cash flow grew 13%.
Portfolio FCF yield fell from 4.4% to 3.7%, partly because Imperial Brands and J M Smucker were sold and Intuit purchased; turnover was 5.4% and TCI 1.08%.

The letter reviews activism and takeover situations at ADP/Pershing Square, Nestlé/Third Point, P&G/Trian and Unilever/Kraft Heinz, generally sceptical of activist playbooks and late management responses.

quotes.point: Smith identifies investor behavior and long-term discipline, not stock selection alone, as the hardest part of the strategy.
quotes.text: the most difficult part of applying the investment strategy suggested by Mr. Munger’s quote, and which we seek to apply, is us.

quotes.point: This captures his scepticism of companies that announce margin targets, buybacks or disposals only after activist or takeover pressure.
quotes.text: If these things are possible and desirable, why weren’t you already doing them?

quotes.point: It explains his negative view of Kraft Heinz’s cost-cutting model in the Unilever bid discussion.
quotes.text: we have never found a business which can cut its way to growth.

implications.text: Treat the letter’s Long Depression analogy, debt-overhang view and low-rate expectation as Terry Smith’s hypothesis, not as a Six South house forecast; test it independently before using it for positioning.
Use the letter’s quality checklist—ROCE, margins, cash conversion, leverage and interest cover—when reviewing global compounder exposure, while noting the portfolio FCF yield fell to 3.7%.
The letter contains no Indonesia-specific analysis; do not extrapolate its UK/US/global conclusions directly to the IDR book.
Flag valuation compression and US dollar weakness—estimated at -5.9% for the Fund in 2017—as performance headwinds, and monitor activism/takeover event risk in holdings.
Remember the letter’s argument that investor behaviour and low turnover matter; assess whether managers can hold quality companies through periods of sector rotation and underperformance.

digests.author: Tom Gayner / Markel Corporation
digests.title: Markel Corporation 2008 Annual Letter to Business Partners
digests.summary: Markel’s 2008 letter to business partners reports a difficult year: book value per share fell 16% to $222.20, the equity portfolio returned a loss of 34%, and the total investment portfolio declined 9.6%, Markel’s worst total return. Despite hurricanes Gustav and Ike and a soft insurance market, Markel reported a 99% combined ratio, low financial leverage and $1.1 billion of cash and short-term investments. Management calls 2008 disappointing but also an opportunity, saying Markel enters 2009 with financial and human capital to pursue specialty insurance and investment opportunities. The letter emphasizes long-term perspective: five-year book value CAGR was 10%, versus a 1.5% annual loss for the S&P 500, while the 20-year book value CAGR was 17%. Management says insurance prices must rise because prices have fallen for years, the economy is in recession, claims may increase, interest rates are low and underwriting profits are necessary. Markel cut equity exposure from over 75% of shareholders’ equity to 49% and increased cash. It also discusses accounting for other-than-temporary impairments, management changes and the One Markel regional structure.
key_points: Book value per share declined 16% to $222.20 in 2008; five-year book value CAGR was 10% and 20-year CAGR was 17%.
The equity portfolio lost 34%; the total investment portfolio declined 9.6%, Markel’s worst total return and first negative return since 1999.
Markel reported a 99% combined ratio despite hurricanes Ike and Gustav and soft insurance pricing; management says margins are too thin and has begun targeted rate increases.
Cash and short-term investments rose to $1.1 billion from $529 million; equity exposure was cut from over 75% of shareholders’ equity to 49%.
Management calls 2008 disappointing but says Markel is prepared for opportunities, expects insurance pricing to improve and believes economies will recover over time.
The letter discusses other-than-temporary impairment as imprecise, says quoted market prices are imperfect guides, and treats comprehensive income/book value as the best proxy for financial success.
Management changes and One Markel: Tony Markel became Vice Chairman, Paul Springman became President and COO, Gerry Albanese became Chief Underwriting Officer, and regional restructuring continued.

quotes.point: Sets the headline performance failure for the year.
quotes.text: In 2008, our book value per share declined 16% to $222.20 per share.

quotes.point: Signals Markel’s view that the insurance pricing cycle must turn.
quotes.text: The time has come to move prices up, and we have started this process.

quotes.point: Highlights the value of liquidity during the market crisis.
quotes.text: cash was our best performing investment.

implications.text: Use the letter’s recession and deleveraging comments as a reminder to check assumptions for restrained consumer and corporate activity, lower debt levels and a slower recovery.
Review North book liquidity and equity exposure against Markel’s move to 49% equity exposure and $1.1 billion of cash; remember its emphasis on margin of safety and gradualism.
Treat the insurance-pricing discussion as external context from Markel’s specialty insurance markets; the text gives no direct IDR or Indonesia read-across.
Separate mark-to-market declines from permanent impairment and document how temporary versus other-than-temporary losses are judged, as Markel does.
Remember Markel’s long-term perspective and that management earned no bonuses after below-goal results; assess performance over multi-year horizons, not just one year.

digests.author: Markel Corporation (Thomas S. Gayner, CIO, among signatories)
digests.title: 2009 Annual Report — Letter to Our Business Partners
digests.summary: Markel’s 2009 letter reports an all-time-high book value per share of about $283, up 27% from $222, alongside a 95% combined ratio on $1.8 billion of earned premiums. Investment returns were 13.2% overall, with equities at 25.7% and fixed income at 9.8%. Gross premiums fell 14% in a soft insurance market. Management describes 2009 as a year of transformation: the One Markel restructuring consolidated regional underwriting and distribution, and the Atlas systems/process project began delivery, with estimated total cost raised to about $190 million from $160 million. Markel International produced a 91% combined ratio and $52 million underwriting profit; Markel Specialty produced 99%. Markel Ventures expanded through Panel Specialists and Ellicott Dredge. The letter emphasizes long-term book-value growth, balance-sheet protection, liquidity and conservative equity exposure—17% of the investment portfolio—while saying Markel will accelerate equity investing when insurance pricing firms and premiums grow. Management makes no prediction on cycle timing and stresses adaptation, management renewal and readiness for improved P&C conditions.
