Underwriting produced a 95% combined ratio on $1.8 billion earned premiums, while gross premiums declined 14% in a soft market.
Investment portfolio returned 13.2% (equities 25.7%, fixed income 9.8%); public equity exposure ended at 17% of the portfolio, below historical averages.
One Markel restructuring and the Atlas systems/process project are central; Atlas total cost estimate rose to about $190 million from $160 million.
Markel International had a 91% combined ratio and $52 million underwriting profit; Markel Specialty had 99%; Markel Ventures added Panel Specialists and Ellicott Dredge.
Management makes no prediction on when the P&C cycle will improve and emphasizes balance-sheet protection, liquidity and management renewal.

quotes.point: Signals the long-term horizon Six South should weigh when judging Markel’s decisions.
quotes.text: We run and operate this business with a view of years and decades as opposed to quarterly and annual comparisons.

quotes.point: Frames conservatism and liquidity as prerequisites for taking advantage of market dislocations.
quotes.text: Protecting the balance sheet is always the most important goal in our investing (as well as in our insurance) operations.

quotes.point: Warns against timing the P&C cycle; readiness matters more than forecasting.
quotes.text: We do not make any predictions as to when this will occur.

implications.text: Remember Markel sees a soft P&C market with no cycle-timing forecast; track underwriting discipline and capital supply rather than assuming a near-term pricing turn.
Use Markel’s balance-sheet-first, long-horizon approach as a comparison for the USD book: check whether positions preserve liquidity for dislocations.

Note Markel International expects opportunities in India, China and Southeast Asia; monitor regional specialty-insurance competition in Southeast Asia without treating it as an Indonesia-specific claim.
Flag the Atlas cost-estimate increase to about $190 million from $160 million as an execution/cost-overrun risk when assessing insurers’ IT transformations.
Track One Markel integration and management-renewal changes as governance/execution items; the letter ties future growth to these changes.

digests.author: Markel Corporation (signed by Alan I. Kirshner, Anthony F. Markel, Steven A. Markel, Richard R. Whitt III, Thomas S. Gayner, F. Michael Crowley)
digests.title: Markel Corporation 2010 Annual Report — To Our Business Partners
digests.summary: Markel's 2010 annual letter to business partners reports record book value per share of $326.36, up 16% from a year earlier, with five- and ten-year compound annual growth rates of 13% and 12%. Operating revenues rose to $2.2 billion from $2.1 billion; earned premiums were $1.7 billion versus $1.8 billion, and the combined ratio was 97% versus 95%, affected by Deepwater Horizon, Chilean earthquakes and IT expenses. Investment return was 7.9%, with equities up 20.8% and fixed income up 5.4%. Management says it remains optimistic on equity returns, has more ideas than money, and has shortened bond maturities in preparation for higher rates. It describes insurance as overcapitalized—roughly $550 billion of U.S. capital against about $400 billion of premiums—and expects the cycle eventually to harden. digests.author: Warren Buffett
digests.title: Berkshire Hathaway 2007 Annual Letter
digests.summary: Berkshire’s 2007 chairman’s letter reports a $12.3 billion gain in net worth and an 11% increase in per-share book value for Class A and Class B shares. Since present management took over, book value has grown from $19 to $78,008, a 21.1% compounded annual rate over 43 years. The 76 operating businesses overall did well, but housing-linked brick, carpet and real-estate brokerage operations had minor and temporary setbacks. Buffett warns that major financial institutions suffered staggering problems from weakened lending practices and the belief that house prices would forever rise; falling prices are exposing financial folly. Insurance had an excellent year, partly because 2007 was the second consecutive year free of major insured catastrophes, but he says that party is over and industry margins, including Berkshire’s, will fall significantly in 2008. Berkshire’s value rests on investments—$141 billion at yearend—and non-insurance earnings, with $59 billion of investments funded by insurance float. The letter describes the Marmon purchase, business-quality yardsticks such as durable moats and capital needs, mistakes including Dexter, segment results, the PetroChina sale, derivatives and U.S. trade/currency concerns.

digests.author: Warren Buffett
digests.title: Berkshire Hathaway Inc. — 2008 Annual Letter
digests.summary: Berkshire Hathaway’s 2008 annual letter reports an $11.5 billion decrease in net worth and a 9.6% decline in per-share book value, which the letter calls the worst year for both Berkshire and the S&P 500 over the table’s 44-year history. Buffett describes a credit crisis that became dysfunctional and then non-functional, with fourth-quarter fear producing a negative-feedback cycle of business contraction and greater fear. He says Treasury and Fed action was essential but warns the unprecedented dosages will bring unwelcome aftereffects, likely including inflation. Berkshire’s insurance float was $58.5 billion and cost less than zero, with a $2.8 billion underwriting profit; utilities and insurance earnings are not correlated with the general economy. The letter defends Clayton Homes’ lending practices and criticizes history-based models and derivatives. Buffett admits a major mistake buying ConocoPhillips near peak energy prices and errors of omission, while stressing ample cash, quality purchases when marked down, and long-term confidence in America. He expects the economy to be in shambles throughout 2009 but says that does not predict stock market direction.

Berkshire stresses ample cash, quality purchases when marked down, and businesses with durable competitive advantages.

digests.author: Warren Buffett
digests.title: Berkshire Hathaway Inc. — 2009 Annual Letter
digests.summary: The 2009 Berkshire letter reports a $21.8 billion gain in net worth and a 19.8% increase in per-share book value, with book value compounding at 20.3% annually since 1965. It compares book value with the S&P 500, noting Berkshire beat the index in all 41 five-year periods ending 2005-09 and in the eleven years the S&P delivered negative results, but warns that its performance advantage has shrunk as size has grown. Buffett restates Berkshire’s principles: avoid businesses whose futures cannot be evaluated, maintain enormous liquidity, decentralize operations, and communicate directly with owners. Insurance remains central: float reached $62 billion and underwriting was profitable for seven consecutive years. GEICO gained market share, while General Re and Ajit Jain’s reinsurance operation are highlighted. MidAmerican utilities and BNSF are framed by a “social compact” with regulators. Manufacturing, service and retail suffered in the recession; NetJets lost $711 million before Dave Sokol’s turnaround; Clayton is constrained by mortgage-rate differentials. Common stocks were carried at $59.0 billion versus $34.6 billion cost, cash was $30.6 billion, and derivatives float was about $6.3 billion. BNSF required issuing about 95,000 shares, or 6.1% dilution.

digests.author: Terry Smith
digests.title: Fundsmith Equity Fund annual letter to shareholders 2018
digests.summary: Terry Smith’s ninth annual letter reports Fundsmith Equity Fund returned +2.2% in 2018 versus -3.0% for the MSCI World Index in sterling and -8.7% for the FTSE 100; cumulative since inception was +269.6%, annualised +17.4%. He argues 2018’s market jitters—trade war fears, Brexit, US rate rises, mid-terms, Italy’s budget, the US shutdown—fell short of turmoil, and that forecasting downturns is unreliable. His principles: bull markets do not die of old age, they climb a wall of worry and narrow as they age; value stocks are best bought after a bear market, not before; and investors need emotional and financial stability to ignore a bear market they cannot predict. The portfolio’s look-through ROCE was 29%, gross margin 65%, operating margin 28%, cash conversion 95% and interest cover 17x. Free cash flow grew 8% and the FCF yield rose from 3.7% to 4.0%. He defends Facebook, discusses Sage and Unilever engagement, reports 13.4% turnover and a 1.09% total cost of investment, and warns against market timing.

digests.author: Terry Smith, CEO, Fundsmith LLP
digests.title: Fundsmith Equity Fund — Annual Letter to Shareholders 2019
digests.summary: Terry Smith's tenth annual letter reports that the Fundsmith Equity Fund's T Class Accumulation shares rose 25.6% in 2019, against 22.7% for the MSCI World Index in sterling and 17.3% for the FTSE 100. Cumulative return since inception on 1 November 2010 was 364.4%, or 18.2% annualised. Sharpe and Sortino ratios since inception were 1.22, versus 0.63 and 0.59 for the index. Top contributors were Microsoft, Estée Lauder, Facebook, PayPal and Philip Morris International; 3M and Colgate Palmolive were sold during the year and Brown-Forman and Clorox were bought. Look-through portfolio metrics show 29% ROCE, 66% gross margin, 27% operating margin and 97% cash conversion, against 17%, 45%, 15% and 84% for the S&P 500. Weighted average free cash flow grew 9%, but the portfolio's free cash flow yield fell from 4.0% to 3.4%, which Smith says makes him nervous. He defends the 'buy good companies, don't overpay, do nothing' approach against value investing, denies any prospect of style drift, and discusses the Woodford gating and fund liquidity.

Look-through quality metrics remain superior to the S&P 500 and FTSE 100, but the portfolio's weighted average FCF yield fell from 4.0% to 3.4% as valuations rose.

Smith rejects the case for a rotation into value stocks and for diversifying across quality and value strategies, and states there will be no style drift at Fundsmith.

On Woodford, he attributes the gating to a daily-dealing open-ended fund holding illiquid and unquoted assets, and notes the Fund's average market cap of £114bn and estimated ability to liquidate 57% in seven days.

quotes.text: it makes us nervous as changes in valuation are finite and reversible

quotes.text: There will be no style drift at Fundsmith.

quotes.text: we estimate we could liquidate 57% of the Fund in seven days

implications.text: The letter's core evidence is that high-ROCE, high-cash-conversion businesses compound through retained earnings, but its own FCF yield fell to 3.4%; keep the quality bias while sizing for the letter's own warning that re-rating is finite and reversible.

Remember the liquidity lesson: a daily-dealing open-ended structure holding illiquid or unquoted assets creates the illusion of liquidity and gates when many investors exit at once. Check redemption terms against underlying asset liquidity on any vehicle Six South holds or considers.

Assess managers on performance after all fees and on the Total Cost of Investment including dealing costs, not on the OCF alone — the letter shows OCF understating costs by up to 65% among large UK funds. Also treat a stated strategy as a commitment to monitor for style drift.

The letter attributes roughly 6% of underperformance in September–October 2019 to a sterling rally off post-referendum lows and to rotation from highly rated quality stocks into lower-rated value stocks. Treat quality-versus-value rotation and rate expectations as live risks, not resolved debates.

On currency, the letter argues exchange rates are neither predictable ('Snakes & Ladders') nor hedgeable, and that revenue exposure matters more than listing venue. When mapping the IDR book, gauge USD revenue exposure rather than listing domicile, and do not budget for currency calls.

digests.author: Markel Corporation leadership

digests.author: Warren Buffett

digests.summary: Berkshire's 2010 letter reports per-share book value up 13%, versus 15.1% for the S&P 500 with dividends, and a 20.2% compounded annual gain since 1965. Buffett highlights the BNSF acquisition, estimating it raises normal pre-tax earning power nearly 40% and after-tax well over 30%, funded with $22 billion of cash while share count rose 6%. He estimates normal earning power at about $17 billion pre-tax and $12 billion after-tax. Berkshire spent $6 billion on property and equipment in 2010, 90% in the U.S., and plans a record $8 billion in 2011. The letter explains intrinsic value through investments ($158 billion), insurance float ($65.8 billion), and non-insurance earnings; float has been cost-free for eight consecutive years. It reviews insurance, manufacturing/service/retail, regulated BNSF/MidAmerican, and finance segments, including Clayton mortgage losses. digests.summary: Markel’s 2014 letter to business partners reviews a “watershed year” and asks “How are we doing, and, what’s next?” Total revenues grew 19% to $5.1 billion from $4.3 billion; gross written premiums were $4.8 billion versus $3.9 billion, with a 95% combined ratio versus 97%. digests.author: Terry Smith
digests.title: Fundsmith Equity Fund Annual Letter 2020
digests.summary: Terry Smith’s January 2021 letter reports Fundsmith Equity Fund’s 2020 T Class return of +18.3%, versus +12.3% for MSCI World and -11.5% for FTSE 100, with annualised return since inception +18.2%. digests.author: Warren Buffett
digests.title: Berkshire Hathaway Inc. — 2013 Annual Letter
digests.summary: Berkshire’s 2013 annual letter reports a $34.2 billion gain in net worth after $1.8 billion of charges from buying minority interests in Marmon and Iscar; per-share book value rose 18.2%. That lagged the S&P 500’s 32.4% gain, which Buffett says fits the pattern of falling short in strong markets while expecting to outperform in down or moderately up years and over full cycles. The year included almost $18 billion of acquisitions—NV Energy and a major Heinz interest—with Heinz structured alongside 3G Capital, including $8 billion of 9% preferred stock and half of the common; Berkshire never intends to sell its Heinz shares. The Powerhouse Five earned a record $10.8 billion pre-tax, smaller non-insurance businesses earned $4.7 billion, and insurance produced an 11th consecutive underwriting profit while float reached $77 billion. Berkshire increased ownership in American Express, Coca-Cola, IBM and Wells Fargo, and holds a Bank of America option. It emphasizes at least $20 billion of cash equivalents, no material short-term obligations, bolt-on acquisitions, and long-term U.S. optimism. It also discloses an $873 million pre-tax loss on Energy Future Holdings bonds and investment lessons from a farm and NYU retail property.
key_points: 2013 net worth gain was $34.2 billion after $1.8 billion of non-economic charges; per-share book value rose 18.2% versus a 32.4% S&P 500 gain.
Berkshire expects to lag in strong markets but outperform in down or moderately up years and over full cycles.
It completed almost $18 billion of acquisitions, including NV Energy and a major Heinz interest structured with 3G Capital.
The Powerhouse Five earned a record $10.8 billion pre-tax; smaller non-insurance businesses earned $4.7 billion.
Insurance operated at an underwriting profit for 11 consecutive years and float reached $77 billion.
Berkshire increased its stakes in American Express, Coca-Cola, IBM and Wells Fargo; each 0.1% ownership increase raises its share of annual earnings by $50 million.
It maintains at least $20 billion of cash equivalents and never incurs material short-term obligations; it also reports an $873 million pre-tax loss on Energy Future Holdings bonds.

quotes.point: Sets expectations for relative performance and cycle-based evaluation.
quotes.text: We expect to fall short, though, in years when the market is strong – as we did in 2013.

quotes.point: Highlights Berkshire’s explicit liquidity and funding discipline.
quotes.text: we will always maintain supreme financial strength, operating with at least $20 billion of cash equivalents and never incurring material amounts of short-term obligations.

quotes.point: Explains preference for substantial non-controlling stakes in excellent businesses.
quotes.text: it’s better to have a partial interest in the Hope diamond than to own all of a rhinestone.

implications.text: Use Berkshire’s stated pattern—lagging in strong markets but outperforming in down or moderately up years—as a reminder to judge strategies over full cycles, not single years.
Check whether North’s quality and liquidity posture reflects Berkshire’s preference for excellent businesses, substantial non-controlling stakes, and strong cash discipline.
Do not read a direct Indonesia or IDR signal into this US-centric letter; treat it only as a global quality-and-liquidity reference.
Stress-test liquidity and short-term obligations against the letter’s standard of supreme financial strength and no material short-term debt.
Remember capital-allocation flexibility—bolt-ons, passive stakes, and repurchases only at meaningful discounts—and avoid EBITDA-style valuation shortcuts.

digests.author: Warren Buffett
digests.title: Berkshire Hathaway Inc. 2014 Annual Letter to Shareholders
digests.summary: Berkshire’s 2014 letter reports a $18.3 billion increase in net worth and an 8.3% rise in per-share book value, with 50-year compounded growth of 19.4% taking book value from $19 to $146,186. Buffett says book value is now a cruder guide to intrinsic value because Berkshire owns more operating businesses carried at cost, so he adds stock-price history; he views the 1,826,163% market-price gain since 1964 as roughly matching intrinsic-value growth. The “Powerhouse Five” earned a record $12.4 billion pre-tax, but BNSF disappointed customers and will spend $6 billion on plant and equipment in 2015. Insurance operated at an underwriting profit for a 12th year, with float at $84 billion and $2.7 billion of 2014 underwriting profit. Berkshire contracted 31 bolt-ons for $7.8 billion, agreed to buy Duracell and Van Tuyl, and increased ownership in American Express, Coca-Cola, IBM and Wells Fargo. Per-share investments rose 8.4% to $140,123 and non-insurance/investment earnings rose 19% to $10,847. Buffett calls America’s best days ahead and admits dawdling on Tesco.
key_points: 2014 net worth rose $18.3 billion; per-share book value rose 8.3%, and 50-year compounded book-value gain was 19.4% ($19 to $146,186).

Buffett says the gap between book value and intrinsic value has widened as Berkshire shifted to owning/operating large businesses; he adds stock-price history and calls the 1,826,163% market gain since 1964 roughly equal to intrinsic-value growth.
Powerhouse Five earned record $12.4 billion pre-tax; BNSF disappointed customers, lost market share, and will spend $6 billion on capex in 2015.
Insurance produced a 12th consecutive underwriting profit; float reached $84 billion and 2014 underwriting profit was $2.7 billion.
Berkshire contracted 31 bolt-ons for $7.8 billion, agreed to buy Duracell and Van Tuyl, and increased stakes in American Express, Coca-Cola, IBM and Wells Fargo.
Per-share investments rose 8.4% to $140,123; non-insurance/investment earnings rose 19% to $10,847; Buffett admits Tesco mistake by dawdling.
Buffett calls a bet on ever-rising U.S. prosperity “very close to a sure thing” and says America’s best days lie ahead.

quotes.point: Management’s long-horizon U.S. optimism underpins the letter’s constructive tone.
quotes.text: America’s best days lie ahead.

quotes.point: Berkshire prefers non-controlling stakes in excellent businesses over full ownership of mediocre ones.
quotes.text: It’s better to have a partial interest in the Hope Diamond than to own all of a rhinestone.

quotes.point: Buffett treats depreciation as a real cost and is skeptical of EBITDA-based valuation.
quotes.text: When CEOs tout EBITDA as a valuation guide, wire them up for a polygraph test.

implications.text: Record Berkshire’s constructive long-horizon U.S. view and expectation of 2015 economic improvement as sentiment input, not a near-term timing signal.
Check North book assumptions on U.S. railroads, industrials and insurance against BNSF’s service/capex issues and Berkshire’s 12-year underwriting-profit and float data.
Remember the document has no Indonesia/IDR coverage; do not map Berkshire’s U.S. optimism directly onto the South book without local evidence.
Use BNSF’s service failure and lost market share as an operational-risk case study; note Berkshire’s stated catastrophe resilience is a management claim, not a guarantee.
Consider Berkshire’s preference for partial interests in wonderful businesses and sensibly priced bolt-ons as a qualitative framework for quality-versus-control, not a trade recommendation.

digests.author: Warren Buffett
digests.title: Berkshire Hathaway Inc. 2015 Annual Letter to Shareholders
digests.summary: The 2015 Berkshire Hathaway letter reports a $15.4 billion gain in net worth and a 6.4% increase in per-share book value, with book value rising from $19 to $155,501 over 51 years, a 19.2% compounded annual rate. Buffett argues that intrinsic value far exceeds book value because accounting writes down losers but never writes up winners; he says Berkshire would be delighted to repurchase shares at 120% of book value. Operating highlights include BNSF’s record $5.8 billion capital expenditure and record $6.8 billion pre-tax income, $13.1 billion earned by the Powerhouse Five, the more than $32 billion cash purchase of Precision Castparts, and a 27% Kraft Heinz holding. Insurance float reached $87.7 billion after 13 consecutive underwriting-profit years totaling $26.2 billion, though the letter warns competition and low rates may pressure industry returns. Berkshire increased its stakes in American Express, Coca-Cola, IBM and Wells Fargo. The letter is constructive on long-term US growth while acknowledging mistakes and the possibility of unprofitable underwriting in any year.
key_points: 2015 net worth gain was $15.4 billion; per-share book value rose 6.4%, and the 51-year compounded annual gain was 19.2%.
Berkshire says intrinsic value far exceeds book value because unrecorded gains at winners are not written up; it would repurchase shares at 120% of book value.
BNSF invested about $5.8 billion in capital expenditures and earned record pre-tax income of $6.8 billion; the Powerhouse Five earned $13.1 billion.
Berkshire bought Precision Castparts for more than $32 billion of cash and owns about 27% of Kraft Heinz.
Insurance float reached $87.7 billion and underwriting profits totaled $26.2 billion over 13 consecutive profitable years.
Berkshire increased ownership in American Express, Coca-Cola, IBM and Wells Fargo; each one-point aggregate ownership increase raises its annual earnings share by about $500 million.

The letter is optimistic on long-term US GDP-per-capita growth but warns that insurance competition and low interest rates may pressure industry returns, and underwriting can be unprofitable in any year.

quotes.point: Supports using intrinsic value rather than book value as the primary valuation anchor.
quotes.text: Today, the large – and growing – unrecorded gains at our “winners” make it clear that Berkshire’s intrinsic value far exceeds its book value.

quotes.point: Explains Berkshire’s preference for substantial non-controlled stakes in excellent businesses.
quotes.text: It’s better to have a partial interest in the Hope Diamond than to own all of a rhinestone.

quotes.point: Frames the letter’s constructive long-term US macro view.
quotes.text: For 240 years it’s been a terrible mistake to bet against America, and now is no time to start.

implications.text: Remember Buffett’s constructive US view rests on 2% real GDP growth and about 0.8% population growth producing about 1.2% per-capita growth; treat it as a long-horizon assumption, not a near-term trade signal.

Use intrinsic value, not book value, as the primary Berkshire valuation anchor; the letter says unrecorded gains make intrinsic value far exceed book value and flags repurchase interest at 120% of book.

Flag that insurance underwriting can be unprofitable in any year, perhaps substantially, and that low rates may steadily reduce float earnings; do not treat 13 years of underwriting profit as a guarantee.

When reviewing earnings, treat stock-based compensation as an expense and be skeptical of compensation-ignoring “earnings” and EBITDA/pre-depreciation valuation guides; the letter also says to add back most amortization but subtract for BNSF’s inadequate depreciation.
Do not map US rail and utility regulation or BNSF/BHE capex economics directly onto the IDR Indonesia book; the document provides no Indonesia-specific data.

digests.author: Terry Smith
digests.title: Fundsmith Equity Fund semi-annual letter
digests.summary: Terry Smith’s July 2022 semi-annual letter reports Fundsmith Equity Fund returned -17.8% in H1 2022, underperforming MSCI World’s -11.3% by 6.5 percentage points, while cumulative since inception was +451.5% and annualised +15.8%. He attributes the market downturn to surging inflation, rising interest rates and recession risk, warning of possible 1970s-style stagflation and saying he is not optimistic about how far rates must rise. He argues supply disruptions, not excess demand, drive inflation and that rates are a blunt tool. The portfolio’s defence is high gross margins—about 60% versus 40% for the average large listed company. He reports portfolio weighted average FCF per share rose 4% in H1 versus Dec 2021 and highlights strong two-year revenue growth at holdings. The portfolio FCF yield rose from 2.7% to 3.6%, taking valuation back to end-2017 levels. He lists top detractors and contributors, says the growth-to-value rotation was underwhelming, and defends TINA and long-term quality compounding over market timing. Turnover was 3.2%.
key_points: H1 2022 Fund return was -17.8% versus MSCI World -11.3%, a 6.5 percentage point underperformance; cumulative since inception was +451.5% and annualised +15.8%.
The letter blames the downturn on surging inflation, consequent rate rises and recession risk, warning of possible stagflation and saying the author is not optimistic on rates.
High gross margins—about 60% versus about 40% for the average large listed company—are presented as the first line of defence against inflation.

Portfolio weighted average FCF per share ended June 2022 4% higher than December 2021, about 8% annualised; strong two-year revenue growth is cited for Adobe, Alphabet, Brown-Forman, Intuit, Microsoft, PayPal and Waters.

Portfolio FCF yield rose from 2.7% to 3.6%, taking valuation back to end-2017; top detractors were PayPal, Meta, IDEXX, Intuit and Microsoft; top contributors were Philip Morris, Novo Nordisk, Brown-Forman, PepsiCo and Waters.
The growth-to-value rotation was underwhelming, energy’s absence cost performance, and the letter defends TINA while rejecting market timing; turnover was 3.2% and Total Cost of Investment 1.05%.

quotes.point: Signals the manager’s cautious view on inflation and the rate path.
quotes.text: I have no insight into how severe or persistent the rise in interest rates will need to be to quell inflation, but I am not optimistic.

quotes.point: Shows the scale of valuation de-rating in the portfolio.
quotes.text: the free cash flow (‘FCF’) yield on the portfolio, which had ended 2021 at 2.7%, increased to 3.6% at the end of June 2022.

quotes.point: Summarises the letter’s long-term quality-compounding stance.
quotes.text: Sooner or later share prices reflect fundamentals, not the other way around.

implications.text: Treat this as a supply-driven inflation and rate-shock view: stress-test for a scenario where rates rise but supply constraints persist, with stagflation risk explicitly noted.
Check North book exposure to long-dated, highly rated equities and to gross-margin resilience; the letter says rising rates hit the most highly rated stocks hardest.
Remember the document contains no Indonesia or IDR-specific analysis; do not extrapolate its global quality and gross-margin claims to the South book without local evidence.
Flag the named detractors and the manager’s admission that PayPal and maybe Intuit had self-inflicted wounds; verify such claims independently rather than relying on the letter.
Note the letter’s argument against selling quality for cash or rotating into value on timing; treat it as the manager’s stance, not an instruction for Six South.

digests.author: Terry Smith, CEO, Fundsmith LLP
digests.title: Fundsmith Equity Fund — Annual Letter to Shareholders 2022 (thirteenth annual letter)
digests.summary: Terry Smith's thirteenth annual letter reports that the Fundsmith Equity Fund's T Class Accumulation shares fell 13.8% in 2022, against a 7.8% fall for the MSCI World Index in sterling, though the Fund remains the best performer in the Investment Association Global sector since inception (+478.2% cumulative, 15.5% annualised). He attributes the setback to the end of 'easy money' — large fiscal deficits and low, zero or negative interest rates traced back to the Greenspan Put — culminating in post-pandemic stimulus and Russia's invasion of Ukraine, which drove inflation and a rapid rise in rates. Higher rates hit longer-dated, highly rated equities hardest: top detractors were Meta, PayPal, Microsoft, IDEXX and Amazon, while defensive names (Novo Nordisk, Philip Morris, PepsiCo, ADP, Mettler-Toledo) contributed. On a look-through basis portfolio ROCE was 32% versus 18% for the S&P 500 and gross margin 64% versus 45%, but weighted free cash flow grew only 1%, the lowest recorded. Year-end FCF yield was 3.2% against 3.4% for the S&P 500, turnover 7.4%. He criticises engagement at Unilever and PayPal and argues share-based compensation should not be excluded from non-GAAP earnings or free cash flow.
key_points: Fund returned -13.8% in 2022 versus -7.8% for MSCI World in sterling, but is still the best performer in the IA Global sector since inception with +478.2% cumulative versus a 179.1% sector average.

Smith blames the drawdown on the end of 'easy money': repeated fiscal and monetary rescue since the 1990s, doubled down in the pandemic, then compounded by the February 2022 invasion of Ukraine and the resulting inflation and rate rises.

Higher rates hurt highly rated, long-duration equities most; the five biggest detractors were Meta (-3.3%), PayPal (-2.5%), Microsoft (-1.8%), IDEXX (-1.7%) and Amazon (-1.5%), while winners were described as 'defensive'.

Look-through portfolio quality remains well ahead of indices: ROCE 32% versus S&P 500 18%, gross margin 64% versus 45%, operating margin 28% versus 18%; but weighted free cash flow grew just 1% and cash conversion fell to 88%.

The portfolio's FCF yield rose from 2.7% to 3.2%, roughly in line with the 3.4% median for the S&P 500; turnover was 7.4% and voluntary dealing cost 0.003% of average value; TCI was 1.05% versus an OCF of 1.04%.

Smith criticises share-based compensation being stripped from non-GAAP earnings and added back in operating cash flow, arguing this distorts multiples (the Intuit versus Microsoft example) and can drive bad acquisitions such as Mailchimp.

On engagement, he says long-standing holders of Unilever and PayPal were ignored while newly arrived activists gained board seats and information-sharing agreements; the fallback when ignored is to sell.

quotes.point: Smith's core macro thesis: policy that suppresses volatility sows the seeds of larger crises, so expecting smooth markets is a mistake.
quotes.text: attempts to expunge volatility from the financial system are actually producing the opposite of the desired effect

quotes.point: Valuation support has improved but he explicitly says this 'does not make them cheap' — no margin-of-safety claim to rely on.
quotes.text: Our companies are more lowly rated than they were a year ago, now being rated roughly in line with the market.

quotes.point: He accepts recession risk from over-tightening and frames it as already reflected in prices, not as a reason to change holdings.
quotes.text: the only type of market which ends in a recession is a bear market

implications.text: Adopt Smith's framing that policy has been 'too lax' and that at some point it becomes 'too tight'; treat recession as a live scenario rather than a tail, and do not assume volatility suppression works.

Use the look-through benchmarks (ROCE 32% vs 18%, gross margin 64% vs 45%) as a quality yardstick, but note the warning signal: weighted FCF growth of only 1% and cash conversion down to 88% — quality of earnings, not just level of returns.

Check whether any holding or comparator we rely on reports non-GAAP EPS or FCF that adds back share-based compensation; the letter's Intuit example shows a 28.4x non-GAAP multiple versus roughly 43x on a comparable basis.

Record the governance point: long-term holders of Unilever and PayPal report being ignored until activists arrived, and the stated remedy when engagement fails is to sell — relevant to how we score management engagement in our own names.

Note the cost discipline argument: 7.4% turnover and voluntary dealing at 0.003% of average value, with TCI only 1bp above OCF — a reminder to judge strategies on net returns rather than headline charges alone.

digests.author: Terry Smith
digests.title: Fundsmith Equity Fund Semi-Annual Letter, July 2023
digests.summary: Terry Smith's July 2023 semi-annual letter reports that the Fundsmith Equity Fund returned 8.5% in the first half of 2023, marginally below the MSCI World Index's 8.9%, while since inception it returned 527.1% cumulative and 15.6% annualised. Top contributors were Meta Platforms, Microsoft, L'Oréal, LVMH and Amadeus; largest detractors were Waters, Estée Lauder, ADP, Mettler-Toledo and Philip Morris. Smith says Meta's share price is much more volatile than its fundamental performance and urges focus on fundamentals rather than commentary. The portfolio's FCF yield fell from 3.2% at end-2022 to about 2.8% at end-June 2023, and he says the portfolio is more expensive than the S&P 500 on this measure. Turnover was 6.2%; voluntary dealing cost £1,192,657, and the Total Cost of Investment was 1.06%. The Fund sold Amazon, and similarly exited Adobe, citing concerns about capital misallocation and investment outside core franchises. Smith describes slower revenue growth at technology companies, resilient healthcare, and pressure on consumer profitability from higher input costs. He says conditions are tougher but expresses no wholesale concern, and reiterates that the Fund does not invest on macroeconomic or geopolitical predictions.
key_points: Fund returned +8.5% in H1 2023 versus MSCI World +8.9%; since inception +527.1% cumulative and +15.6% annualised.
Top contributors: Meta +3.1%, Microsoft +2.6%, L'Oréal +1.5%, LVMH +1.1%, Amadeus +1.0%; top detractors: Waters -1.2%, Estée Lauder -1.2%, ADP -0.6%, Mettler-Toledo -0.4%, Philip Morris -0.4%.
Portfolio FCF yield fell from 3.2% at end-2022 to about 2.8% at end-June 2023; Smith says the portfolio is more expensive than the S&P 500 on this measure.
Turnover was 6.2%; voluntary dealing cost £1,192,657, the OCF was 1.04%, and the Total Cost of Investment was 1.06%.
The Fund sold Amazon citing potential capital misallocation and grocery retail expansion contrary to stated investment principles; a similar thought process led to exiting Adobe.

Technology revenue growth slowed, healthcare remained resilient, and consumer profitability faced input-cost pressure; Smith calls conditions tougher but not a wholesale concern and says the Fund does not invest on macro or geopolitical predictions.

quotes.point: Valuation context: portfolio FCF yield fell to about 2.8% and is above the S&P 500 on this measure.
quotes.text: our portfolio is more expensive than the S&P 500 Index on this measure

quotes.point: Smith's argument for focusing on business fundamentals rather than share-price volatility and commentary.
quotes.text: it is much more volatile than its fundamental performance

quotes.point: Summarises the operating backdrop: slower top-line growth and margin pressure from input costs.
quotes.text: conditions are tougher and our companies are mostly having to cope with slower revenue growth and/or higher input costs

implications.text: Remember the author explicitly avoids investing on macroeconomic or geopolitical predictions; do not treat this letter as a rates, recession or geopolitics signal.
Check North global holdings' FCF yield and cash conversion against the letter's note that Fundsmith's portfolio FCF yield fell to about 2.8% and is more expensive than the S&P 500 on that measure.
Review capital-allocation discipline in North names, especially expansions outside core franchises; Fundsmith sold Amazon and Adobe after such concerns.
Monitor large-tech revenue slowdown and consumer gross-margin pressure from input costs highlighted in the letter.
No Indonesia or IDR-specific content appears in the letter; avoid inferring South book actions from this document.

digests.author: Thomas S. Gayner, Co-Chief Executive Officer (letter signed also by Alan I. Kirshner, Anthony F. Markel, Steven A. Markel, and Richard R. Whitt, III)
digests.title: Markel 2017 Annual Letter to Business Partners
digests.summary: Markel's 2017 annual letter reviews a year it calls 'transformational' and 'watershed.' Total revenues rose 8% to $6.1 billion, insurance premiums rose 10% to $4.2 billion, and Markel Ventures revenues rose 10% to $1.3 billion. Record insured catastrophes produced an underwriting loss of $205 million versus a $317 million profit in 2016; CATs added 13 points to the 105% combined ratio. The company paid $159 million of claims from these events, with total expected losses of $565 million, and says losses were in line with major-CAT estimates. Markel acquired SureTec, State National, and Costa Farms using cash and no dilutive equity, increasing size and revenue footprint by about a quarter. Public equity holdings returned 26%, fixed income 3%, and the total portfolio 10%; comprehensive income was $1.2 billion. Management reiterates its long-standing diversification and specialization strategy, four-step equity approach, low-cost internal investment management, conservative financial practices, and expectation of underwriting profits in 2018. It also cites a $300 million 30-year 4.30% debt raise and a $402 million equity increase from the U.S. tax-rate reduction.
key_points: 2017 set a record for insured catastrophe losses; Markel reported an underwriting loss of $205 million versus a $317 million profit in 2016, with CATs adding 13 points to its 105% combined ratio.
Total revenues were $6.1 billion, up 8%; insurance premiums were $4.2 billion, up 10%; Markel Ventures revenues were $1.3 billion, up 10%; comprehensive income was $1.2 billion versus $667 million.
Markel acquired SureTec, State National, and Costa Farms with cash and issued no dilutive equity; the deals increased size and revenue footprint by about a quarter.

Investment results included 26% returns on public equities, 3% on fixed income, and 10% total portfolio returns; public equity holdings produced more than $1 billion of unrealized gains, realized gains, and dividends.

Management reaffirms diversification and specialization, its four-step equity selection approach, low-cost internal investment management, conservative financing, and an expectation of underwriting profits in 2018.
Markel raised $300 million of 30-year fixed-rate financing at 4.30% and increased shareholders' equity by $402 million from the U.S. corporate tax-rate reduction.

quotes.point: Anchors the letter's claim that strategy has not changed since its 1986 IPO.
quotes.text: our corporate strategy is one of diversification and specialization.

quotes.point: Claims-paying culture is central to the CAT-loss discussion.
quotes.text: We keep our promises.

quotes.point: Signals expected underwriting profit in 2018 after the 2017 CAT-driven loss.
quotes.text: We remain fully committed to the discipline of underwriting profits.

implications.text: Track post-CAT property insurance pricing; the letter says Markel can seek property risks in a 'post CAT environment of higher pricing and prospectively better financial returns.'
Use Markel's cash-funded acquisitions and record claims payments as a capital-strength screen for North insurance exposures; it issued no dilutive equity while paying record CAT claims.
Do not extrapolate this U.S./global insurer letter to the IDR book; it contains no Indonesia-specific data or portfolio holdings.
Flag CAT sensitivity in any insurance-related exposure: CATs added 13 points to Markel's combined ratio and drove a $205 million underwriting loss.
Remember Markel's four equity criteria—returns on capital, management talent and integrity, reinvestment/acquisition skill, and reasonable price—as a quality checklist, not a recommendation.

digests.author: Richard R. Whitt, III and Thomas S. Gayner
digests.title: Markel 2018 Annual Letter to Business Partners
digests.summary: Markel’s 2018 annual letter calls the year “good, but not great.” Revenues reached a record $6.8 billion versus $6.1 billion in 2017, but the company reported a comprehensive loss of $376 million versus comprehensive income of $1.2 billion, citing investment-market downdrafts and high insured catastrophes. It says economic value stands at a new record and shares outstanding ended lower. The letter details Markel’s Insurance Linked Securities strategy, including acquisitions of CATCo, Nephila and State National, and describes ILW coverage and binary loss outcomes. It discloses U.S. and Bermuda inquiries into CATCo loss reserves recorded in late 2017 and early 2018, says the investigation is ongoing, and acknowledges CATCo’s initial catastrophe loss estimates were too low. Insurance GWP was $5.8 billion with a 98% combined ratio; investments returned -1.0%; Markel Ventures revenues were $1.9 billion with $170 million EBITDA. Management emphasizes a long-term, five-year framework, diversification and specialization, and says 2019 risk-transfer prices are higher.
key_points: 2018 revenues set a record at $6.8 billion, but comprehensive loss was $376 million versus $1.2 billion income in 2017, driven by investment markdowns and catastrophes.
Insurance gross written premiums were $5.8 billion and the combined ratio improved to 98% from 105%, despite six points of catastrophe losses.
Markel built its ILS platform through CATCo, Nephila and State National; CATCo faced U.S. and Bermuda inquiries into loss reserves and the investigation remained ongoing.
CATCo’s initial estimates for 2017 and 2018 catastrophe losses proved too low; ILW contracts can have binary outcomes that complicate reserve setting.
Investments returned -1.0% in 2018, with equities -3.5% versus -4.4% for the S&P 500 and fixed income 1.3%; five-year equity return was 9.7%.
Markel Ventures reported 2018 revenues of $1.9 billion and EBITDA of $170 million; five-year revenues were $6.4 billion and EBITDA $709 million.
Management ties most incentive compensation to five-year results and emphasizes a long-term owner mindset; it says 2019 risk-transfer prices are higher than the prior two years.

quotes.point: Management frames mixed results candidly, setting the tone for the letter.
quotes.text: 2018 was a good, but not great, year.

quotes.point: Regulatory and reserve risk in the ILS operation is material and unresolved.
quotes.text: we received inquiries from U.S. and Bermuda authorities into loss reserves recorded in late 2017 and early 2018 at CATCo and its subsidiaries.

quotes.point: Pricing is a potential tailwind for ILS/reinsurance, though the letter does not guarantee profitability.
quotes.text: the prices for transferring these risks are higher in 2019 than what they’ve been in the two previous years.

implications.text: Monitor CATCo’s reserve inquiry and any ILS loss-estimate revisions; binary ILW contracts can swing from no loss to total loss, so stress-test any ILS or reinsurance exposure.
Keep Markel and insurance-linked exposure framed on five-year returns and pricing; note 2018’s comprehensive loss was driven by mark-to-market and catastrophes, not solely underwriting.
The letter contains no Indonesia-specific data; do not extrapolate IDR or South book changes from this document alone.
Record catastrophe losses and higher 2019 risk-transfer prices may inform reinsurance cost assumptions, but the letter provides no broad macroeconomic forecast.
Remember management ties incentive compensation to five-year results and urges a long-term owner mindset; avoid overreacting to single-year mark-to-market swings.
